📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Electric truck operator Nevoya is expanding its deal with Meta with the fresh deployment of 25 Class 8 battery-electric trucks on the Interstate 10 (I-10) between San Bernardino, California and Phoenix, Arizona … but Meta won’t be shipping any products.

The second major trucking deal between Facebook parent tech giant Meta and electric truck operator Nevoya will put 25 newly introduced battery-electric semis on I-10, running freight between San Bernardino, California and Phoenix, Arizona. But Meta isn’t buying trucks, hiring drivers or shipping its own products. Instead, Zuck’s company helping pay for someone else’s cleaner freight through environmental attribute certificates (EACs), a carbon credit mechanism that lets companies claim the emissions benefits of electric trucking without operating the trucks themselves.

According to recent reports, “Coming back to Nevoya for a second corridor reflects what we look for in our value chain work: partners that can scale, and agreements we can repeat, said Devon Lake, Head of Net Zero Strategy, Meta. “Freight is part of the emissions footprint of building and operating our data centers, and multi-year commitments like this help address our scope 3 emissions and make electric trucking available and competitive on the routes that serve the regions where we build.”.

Meta was one of several buyers in the DC-based Center for Green Market Activation (GMA) buyers’ alliance. The group’s collective EAC purchases supported Nevoya’s initial 63-truck deployment on the Houston–Dallas corridor back in May. This new Agreement, however, is a standalone deal between Nevoya and Meta only, and gives Meta an established framework to open more electric truck corridors in the future.

This clever application of these agreements is what makes the Dallas-Houston run stand out, with GMA calling it, “the first large-scale application of book and claim to zero-emission trucking.” The manufacturer adds that this arrangement helps client companies overcome existing barriers to EV adoption while enabling Nevoya to deploy new trucks, “where they deliver the strongest commercial and operational value.”.

Latest Update: The 10 Best Smartwatches for Men, Tested by Gear Editors

📅 31 Jul 2020 | ⏱️ 27 min read (5388 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Menshealth

⏱️ ~27 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • AT MEN'S HEALTH, we love a good fitness tracker—but let’s be honest, they’re not exactly stylish.
  • With the Galaxy Watch9, Samsung didn’t mess with a good thing.
  • Recent findings suggest that one of the most notable latest additions is the Vitals tool, which learns your normal range for things like heart rate and blood oxygen, then flags you when something’s off.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AT MEN'S HEALTH, we love a good fitness tracker—but let’s be honest, they’re not exactly stylish. Most of them look great with running shorts and a workout tee—but less so when you’re in a crisp dress shirt and tailored trousers. That’s where the best smartwatches for men come in. They bridge the gap between performance tech and actual style—tracking your heart rate and steps without clashing with your fit. A great smartwatch can go from your 6 a.m. run to your 8 p.m. cocktail hour without missing a beat. Some, like the TAG Heuer Connected, look so sleek you could wear them for a black-tie event and look like you belong on the cover of a magazine. We’ve tested dozens to find the ones that deliver that perfect balance of design, durability, and data.

With the Galaxy Watch9, Samsung didn’t mess with a good thing. The aluminum case, “squircle” shape, and bright 3,000-nit screen all carry over from the Watch8 that was our previous favorite—so at a glance you’d be hard-pressed to tell them apart. The key changes are under the hood: a bigger battery, a more power-efficient processor, and a smarter set of health tools that turn your sleep and workout data into advice you can act on.

Recent findings suggest that one of the most notable latest additions is the Vitals tool, which learns your normal range for things like heart rate and blood oxygen, then flags you when something’s off. A jump in your resting heart rate or skin temperature, for instance, can signal a cold before you feel it—keep in mind these should be anecdotal. The other new features are for the data-driven crowd. A Heart Health Score rolls your sleep, activity, and blood-pressure trends into a single read on how your lifestyle is affecting your heart, with tips to improve it. My sleep schedule has been all over the place lately, making me feel lethargic at certain parts of the day, and the Watch9 has been recommending I go to bed earlier. Finally, a Fitness Index charts your body composition, cardio, endurance, flexibility, and strength on a spider graph so you can see where you’re strong and where you’re lagging.

There are carryovers from the Watch8 too, including the Running Coach that builds a plan off a 12-minute test run, with well-structured workouts, and the Antioxidant Index, which reads the carotenoid levels in your skin for a rough sense of your fruit and vegetable intake (to be taken with a grain of salt).

In a brief head-to-head test against the Apple Watch Series 11, the Watch9’s heart rate held within a few beats on runs and walks. I’ve been following a Couch to 5K program for the past four weeks, and the heart-rate readings during each run are reliable enough to pace by. Daily Cardio Load has also been a big help, nudging me to dial it back instead of pushing myself too hard, too soon.

Samsung dropped the older Exynos chip for Qualcomm’s Snapdragon Wear Elite, and everything feels snappier, from starting a workout to pulling up a stat mid-run to talking to Google’s Gemini. Now you just lift your wrist to say a command, rather than first saying a wake word.

The Watch9 keeps the excellent Dynamic Lug System, making it comfortable enough to sleep in, and its premium-yet-friendly design moves from a morning run to a business-casual meeting without looking out of place. It comes in 40mm and 44mm sizes with a wider band lineup, including Sport, Fabric, and a two-tone Misty. The battery is bigger on paper—390mAh on the 40mm, a 20 percent bump, and in my testing it still lands around a day of use. At $379.99, Samsung’s newest model costs a bit more than the Watch8 did at launch, but you’re getting the smartest, most feature-packed version yet.

Read More: Best Fitness Trackers for Men.

It has been revealed that the Apple Watch SE used to be the Apple Watch you bought because you couldn’t justify spending more. Apple changed that with the SE 3 by adding an always-on display, the S10 chip, double-tap and wrist-flick gestures, 5G cellular on cellular models, and health features like Sleep Score and breathing irregularity detection through the Vitals app.

In a recent development, over several weeks of testing, the SE 3 held up as a daily driver without feeling like a compromise. The always-on display made a real difference while exercising, and performance felt snappy across the board—from launching workouts to setting timers with on-device Siri. Fast charging is the other underrated upgrade. A 15-minute top-up while showering in the morning was enough to carry the watch through the rest of the day and overnight for sleep tracking.

Recent findings suggest that after a rough night (67 out of 100), I could see exactly how that Sleep Score was calculated and adjusted accordingly, scoring a 90 the next night. The Vitals app runs in the background and tracks wrist temperature and respiratory rate without any input. It hasn’t flagged anything yet, but that kind of passive monitoring adds value over time.

The upcoming Series 12 is also available at $399. For the extra $150, it adds an ECG app, a Blood Oxygen app, and hypertension notifications, none of which the SE 3 has. It also takes a background heart rate reading every five seconds, and its Readiness app turns recent activity, training load, vitals, and sleep into a single score.

The Series 12’s display reaches 2,000 nits (the SE 3 gets to 1,000), the bezels are thinner, and the screen area is larger. Battery life is rated at 24 hours compared to the SE 3’s 18 hours, and five minutes on the charger gives up to 10 hours of sleep tracking, where the SE 3 gets up to eight hours from eight minutes. The Series 12 also adds a water temperature sensor and a depth gauge to six meters for snorkeling.

It has been revealed that we recommend the Series 12 if you use a watch to follow training load and recovery, if you swim or snorkel, or if you want more advanced health tracking features. But the SE 3 is the call if you want notifications and standard workout and sleep tracking on an Apple Watch that still has an always-on display, and you’re on more of a budget.

Read More: Apple Watch SE 3 Review.

If you want a GPS running watch that nails the fundamentals and is relatively affordable, the Coros Pace 4 should be at the top of your list. At $249, it competes on accuracy, battery life, and display quality with watches that cost significantly more, and at 40 grams with a silicone strap, it’s light enough to forget you’re wearing it.

The biggest upgrade from the Pace 3 is the AMOLED display, which is sharp and easy to read in bright sunlight. Battery life actually improved despite the brighter screen, jumping to 31 hours in max GPS mode with all satellite systems active, or 24 hours with always-on display enabled. A quick charge while you’re showering or eating a meal should top it off.

Industry observers note that GPS tracking is where Coros built its reputation, and the Pace 4 delivers. Dual-frequency satellite support promises clean, accurate tracks that hold up even alongside buildings and under tree cover. The Pace 4 also features voice logging, so after finishing a run, the watch prompts you to record your thoughts, which get transcribed and saved in the Coros app. The watch also uses breadcrumb navigation rather than full maps, so if you rely on turn-by-turn directions while exploring fresh routes, you’ll want to step up to the Coros Apex or a Garmin with offline maps.

Read More: The Gear I Used to Train for My Longest Race Yet.

Recent findings suggest that our contributing editor and watch expert Ted Stafford, who styles every Men’s Health cover, was seriously impressed by the TAG Heuer Connected Calibre E5. “I was impressed by how well the E5 straddles the line between traditional style and modern innovation,” he notes. “It wears beautifully on the wrist, with a sleek, stylish design and a comfort-first build. Its intuitive interface also makes it refreshingly simple to navigate, even on the move or during high-intensity activities.”.

Sources indicate that in fact, Stafford recently met with Tag Heuer’s team in Boston to test the Connected Calibre E5. During his 5K run, he appreciated how easy it was to glance at messages, check his heart rate, and accurately track his activity—all without slowing down. He also noted that the stainless bracelet stayed comfortable and secure the whole time. Another standout feature is the ability to customize the watch face. “Whether you’re in the mood for a sporty Carrera or a bold Formula 1 look, the E5 lets you effortlessly switch styles to match your day,” he says. “This and all the other unique tech offerings make having a connected watch a win-win for me.”.

What really makes the E5 shine, though, is how much it packs under the hood. You get dual-band GPS for pinpoint tracking, heart-rate and blood-oxygen sensors, and full sleep and stress tracking that rivals top fitness-focused wearables. The new TAG Heuer OS runs smoother than ever, with cleaner visuals and tighter iPhone integration for those in the Apple ecosystem. Plus, it’s built like a tank with 50 meters of water resistance, a sapphire crystal display, and your choice of steel or titanium cases. Battery life clocks in at about two days of regular use, and fast charging gets you back to full in around 30 minutes.

The Apple Watch Ultra 4 keeps the 49mm titanium case of the Ultra 3 and replaces the sensor on the back. The new Health Sensing System adds a circular optical sensing array, larger and more efficient LEDs for heart rate readings, and more surface area touching the skin for ECG readings. Earlier models took background heart rate readings every five minutes. The Ultra 4 takes one every five seconds and shows it in a new heart rate complication, which is a data point you pin to the watch face. Faster readings also let the watch measure heart rate variability (the variation in time between heartbeats) as often as every five minutes while you’re at rest.

The Ultra 4 also adds Readiness, which combines Fitness, Vitals, and Sleep Score into a rating from 1 to 10 for how prepared your body is for the day. Readiness needs several consecutive nights of sleeping with the watch before it starts scoring. The S11 chip makes the watch feel quicker and powers a new step counter and better Siri, which our tester used to set timers more often than ever.

Apple rates the battery at up to 50 hours of normal use and up to 84 hours in Low Power Mode, with up to 18 hours of continuous workout tracking. In testing, the first charge lasted two nights of sleep. When the battery dropped to about 10 percent one night, our tester was almost three-quarters charged by the time he had brushed his teeth, gotten into bed, and set an alarm. Apple says 15 minutes on the charger gives up to 18 hours of use. Adventure watches from other brands can last weeks between charges, so the Ultra 4 still trails them.

The Ultra 4 costs $799 and the Series 12 costs $399. Both have the same sensors and health features, so the Ultra 4’s advantages are the bigger battery, the 49mm case, and adventure features like precision dual-frequency GPS, emergency SOS via satellite, and diving to 40 meters.

Read More: Apple Watch Ultra 4 Review.

It has been revealed that when it comes to premium running watches, the latest Suunto Race (the Race 2) packs a serious punch at $499—or $599 for the Titanium Trail version. The display is larger and brighter than the Race 1 while being thinner. That said, at 49mm, the Race 2 isn’t a small watch. Men’s Health Senior Gear and Reviews Editor Ryan Brower put it to the test, noting: “While I’ve enjoyed testing it, the Race 2 would be nice to have in a smaller size.”.

That bigger size, though, makes room for a faster processor and an impressive 55 hours of battery life in GPS mode (or up to 30 days with daily use and no training). “The battery claims really hold,” Brower says. “I’ve only had to charge it a couple of times throughout months of testing. To be fair, I don’t wear it every day, but I did for a few stretches to get a sense of it.” Another big improvement is the redesigned charging clip, which Brower found far more effective and reliable than previous Suunto models that didn’t always connect easily.

According to recent reports, performance-wise, the Race 2 delivers more than 115 sport modes. Brower put many of those programs through their paces—treadmill running, running, trail running, strength training, hiking, climbing, rowing (technically paddling), and even surfing—and each one worked smoothly, serving up plenty of useful metrics. GPS tracking proved fairly accurate, and features like training load and recovery provided deeper insights when synced with the Suunto Coach or other training apps. Building a regimen and letting the watch help implement it, Brower notes, “can be a great tool for runners.”.

It has been revealed that the Race 2 leans into a rugged aesthetic with its large round case and durable polymer or titanium build. Its style clearly favors sport and outdoor fits, so the 49mm case can feel oversized or out of place in formal or office clothes. The standard strap is a breathable silicone, perfect for sweaty workouts or trail runs, and the Titanium Trail model adds a premium case finish for those who want a more elevated look in casual settings.

Read More: Garmin Vs. Apple Watch.

According to recent reports, the Pixel Watch 5 looks almost identical to the Pixel Watch 4. It comes in the same 41mm and 45mm sizes, with a domed Actua 360 display under scratch-resistant Gorilla Glass that reaches 3,000 nits at its brightest. Most of the changes are inside and in the software. Google says the new watch is 20 percent faster than the Pixel Watch 4, and it’s built around Gemini. Raise your wrist to talk to the assistant, and the watch face brings up things like flight info and your ETA when you need them.

The Pixel Watch 5 can detect a loss of pulse and prompt a call to emergency services. Satellite SOS lets you contact emergency services and upgrade family from remote areas without cell service, and Google includes it free for two years after activation. Fall Detection, Car Crash Detection, and Safety Check are back, too. Safety Check shares your location with emergency contacts if a timer runs out during a solo run or a late walk home and you don’t respond.

It has been revealed that fresh this generation, the Pixel Watch 5 can show your blood pressure trends and track signs of insulin resistance over the course of a month. Google is clear that neither is a medical reading or a diagnosis, but both can flag patterns to bring up with your doctor. You also get the ECG app, irregular heart rhythm alerts, SpO2, HRV, skin temperature, and a nightly Sleep Score from what Google calls its most accurate sleep tracking yet. Each morning, Morning Brief combines your sleep recap, readiness, and the weather on one screen.

Google calls the watch’s dual-frequency GPS its best yet. It uses machine learning to keep runs through tall downtown buildings and hikes under thick tree cover on track. The watch tracks more than 50 activities. You can build strength sessions with exact reps, weights, and rest timers, and get audio and visual guidance as you go. A Google Health Premium subscription, which includes three free months, adds a Gemini-powered coach that adjusts your blueprint around your schedule.

Google rates the battery at up to 30 hours for the 41mm model and up to 40 hours for the 45mm. That means charging most days, but the included Quick Charge Dock adds 15 hours in 15 minutes, so a short top-up in the morning gets you through a night of sleep tracking. The watch only works with Android phones, and at $399.99, it costs $50 more than the Pixel Watch 4 did at launch. If you’re an Android user who wants the strongest safety features on any smartwatch, it’s still the one to beat.

In a recent development, the Fēnix 9 is Garmin’s premium multisport GPS watch, built for people who take their training and outdoor adventures seriously. It comes in 43mm, 47mm, and 51mm cases, with the 43mm model being styled for smaller wrists. Every version has an AMOLED display with a titanium bezel and a scratch-resistant sapphire lens, and it offers a much brighter screen than the Fēnix 8’s. The watch is tested to U.S. military standards for heat, shock, and water resistance, and it’s rated for recreational dives to 40 meters.

Industry observers note that navigation has always been Garmin’s forte, and it’s where the latest model stands apart. Full-color topographic maps come preloaded, and the Fēnix 9 has twice the RAM of the Fēnix 8 and an updated map engine that pans 30 percent faster. Storage doubles to 64GB, which holds twice as many maps as before plus up to 7,000 songs from Spotify, Deezer, or Amazon Music. Tell the watch how far you want to go, and dynamic round-trip routing suggests a loop that brings you back. If you go off course, it maps a new route with the same mileage. NextFork shows the distance to the next trail junction and the name of the trail, ClimbPro shows current and upcoming climbs on downloaded courses, and SatIQ adjusts GPS accuracy to save battery.

According to recent reports, garmin rates the 43mm model at up to 10 days in smartwatch mode. That's a different category from any Apple Watch or Samsung Galaxy Watch, and it means far less battery anxiety day to day. You don’t have to be quite as strategic when you charge as you would with other smartwatches.

Industry observers note that the training tools go deeper than ever before, too. Newly introduced stamina features show how your endurance holds up over different distances and help you manage your effort during a race. Garmin Epic combines several days of activities into one summary in the Garmin Connect app, which is useful for a backpacking trip or a training camp. Rowers get VO2 max and power metrics, and rucking workouts let you enter your pack weight.

Returning features include Training Readiness, which scores your sleep, recovery, and training load each morning, along with HRV status, sleep coaching, PacePro race pacing, and an ECG app. A built-in speaker and microphone let you take calls from your wrist when the watch is paired with your iPhone or Android phone, and there's a built-in LED flashlight.

In a recent development, the 43mm Fēnix 9 is pricey at $999.99, and more advanced connectivity features like inReach satellite messaging, SOS, and LTE calling require the more expensive Fēnix 9 Pro, so the standard model relies on your paired phone to send your live location if it detects an incident. But for athletes who log serious miles across multiple sports and want one watch that handles all of it, the Fēnix 9 is the way to go.

We got our hands on the G-Shock Move, and this thing is a beast—in the best way possible. Built with G-Shock’s signature toughness, it feels indestructible yet surprisingly comfortable on the wrist. I ran, lifted, and hiked with it, and it handled everything without a hiccup. Inside, you’ve got serious hardware: GPS, heart-rate monitoring, altimeter, compass, thermometer, and a gyroscope that tracks every stride, step, and elevation change with precision.

What really impressed me was how capable it felt in different conditions. I tracked a few long runs with GPS fully active, and the data stayed consistent and accurate the whole time—no weird pace spikes or drop-offs. The battery life held up too; even when I pushed it hard, I still got several days before needing a recharge. And when it does run low, the solar-assisted charging converts sunlight into extra power, adding several hours—or even a day or two—of runtime if you’re outdoors. It’s rated for 200 meters of water resistance, so swimming, rain, and sweat are all fair game.

Living up to its name, the G-Shock Move supports more than a dozen sports, from trail running and cycling to gym training and open-water swimming, while also monitoring sleep, recovery, and blood-oxygen levels. The display’s bright and easy-to-read mid-workout, and the interface feels intuitive enough to switch modes on the fly. For guys who demand a watch that’s as tough and versatile as they are, this one’s the real deal.

Sources indicate that the Fitbit Edge is a fitness tracker first, with just enough smartwatch features to cover the basics. You can read notifications, send quick replies, set alarms, control your music, get turn-by-turn directions from Google Maps, and find your phone. But there are no calls, no contactless payments, no voice assistant, and no app store.

It has been revealed that that limited feature set is why the battery lasts up to seven days and charges back to full in 90 minutes. The rounded display is also 45 percent bigger and more than 40 percent brighter than on previous Fitbits, and it reveals your stats and coaching cues at a glance.

According to recent reports, built-in GPS and an altimeter let you map outdoor runs, rides, and hikes and track how much you climb without bringing your phone. The Edge also recognizes workouts automatically, so a walk or run still counts if you forget to start it. The tracker records heart rate, HRV, SpO2, breathing rate, skin temperature, and resting heart rate. Each night it also tracks your sleep stages and gives you a Sleep Score. High and low heart rate alerts and Irregular Rhythm Notifications flag potential heart concerns.

Recent findings suggest that A Google Health Premium membership, which comes with three free months and then costs $9.99 a month, unlocks a Gemini-powered coach that builds a training initiative around your schedule. It also adds blood pressure and insulin resistance trends. Google says neither is a clinical reading nor a screening tool, but both can flag patterns to discuss with your doctor.

At $179.99, the Edge works with both iPhone and Android phones and comes with small and large bands in the box. It’s a good fit if a full smartwatch is more than you need but you still want to see texts and directions on your wrist. If you want calls, payments, and apps, look at the Pixel Watch 5 or Apple Watch SE 3 instead.

Recent findings suggest that read More: Google Fitbit Air Vs. Fitbit Edge.

Industry observers note that yes, but how much they can do depends on whether the watch has cellular. Any watch with built-in GPS can track workouts, heart rate, and sleep without your phone. Some, like the Garmin Fēnix 9, also store maps and music so you can navigate and listen on a phone-free run.

For texts, calls, and notifications, you need a cellular model. The Apple Watch Ultra 4 comes with cellular built in, while the Apple Watch SE 3 and Series 12 offer it as an upgrade. Watches without cellular, along with fitness trackers like the Fitbit Edge, stop getting notifications once you're out of range of your phone. Some options like the Ultra 4 also add satellite SOS, which lets you reach emergency services when there's no cell service at all.

It has been revealed that smartwatches are more accurate than ever, thanks to newer optical sensors, more LEDs, and more sensor area touching your skin. Most of today’s flagship watches from Apple, Google, Samsung, and Garmin are reliable enough for everyday tracking and most workouts. A chest strap is still the most precise option, though, so pair one with your watch for hard intervals or races. The Garmin Fēnix 9, for example, works with Garmin's HRM 600. Over time, trends in your heart rate are more useful than any single reading, so wear your watch consistently.

Most full-featured smartwatches last one to two days on a charge, while fitness-focused watches can go a week or more. The Google Pixel Watch 5 is rated at up to 30 hours for the 41mm model and up to 40 hours for the 45mm, and the Apple Watch Ultra 4 is rated at up to 50 hours (up to 84 hours in low power mode). Garmin rates the 43mm Fēnix 9 at up to 10 days, the Fitbit Edge lasts up to seven, and the Suunto Race 2 can go up to 30 days with daily use when you’re not tracking workouts.

According to recent reports, your actual battery life depends on how you use the watch, since GPS tracking, continuous heart rate monitoring, and an always-on display all drain it faster. If you track your sleep, look for fast charging, too. Apple says 15 minutes on the charger gives the Ultra 4 up to 18 hours of use, and 15 minutes on Google’s Quick Charge Dock adds 15 hours to the Pixel Watch 5.

According to recent reports, fabric and silicone bands are best for workouts because they’re lightweight, breathable, and dry quickly. Woven nylon and elastic straps adjust easily and won’t dig into your wrist mid-run, though they can hold onto odor and need an occasional wash. Metal bracelets in stainless steel, titanium, or aluminum give a smartwatch a polished, traditional look for the office or a formal event, but they feel heavy during workouts and can trap sweat. Leather bands dress up a watch for work or dinner and mold to your wrist over time. They’re not a great option for workouts, though, because sweat and water can warp or stain them.

A lifestyle or hybrid smartwatch is the best fit for most offices, because it’s sleek enough for business casual and still tough enough for the gym. The Samsung Galaxy Watch9 is a good example, with a slim aluminum case that works with casual, sporty, and business-casual outfits. If you dress up more often, a luxury smartwatch like the TAG Heuer Connected Calibre E5 pairs a stainless steel case and sapphire crystal with performance tracking, and it looks right with a suit. Adventure watches like the Suunto Race 2 and Garmin Fēnix 9 have larger cases built for trail running, hiking, and multisport training, while rugged watches like the Casio G-Shock Move are shock- and water-resistant for tough conditions. Both are better suited to the weekend than a client meeting.

In a recent development, every smartwatch should handle notifications, music controls, and heart rate and sleep tracking. Built-in GPS is worth having if you run, ride, or hike without your phone. Beyond the basics, the features worth paying for depend on how you train. Runners and outdoor athletes should look for dual-frequency GPS and offline maps, like those on the Garmin Fēnix 9 and Suunto Race 2. If you want guidance, look for training plans that adapt to your progress, like Garmin Coach or the Gemini-powered coach in Google Health Premium. For recovery, look for HRV, sleep scores, and readiness scores, which the Apple Watch Ultra 4, Pixel Watch 5, and Fēnix 9 all offer. If you want to leave your phone at home, look for an onboard voice assistant like Siri or Gemini, contactless payments, and LTE for calls and texts.

Industry observers note that bracelets (or metal bands) are best for work, formal occasions, and everyday wear. They give your smartwatch a more polished, traditional-watch look—great for dressing up or blending your tech into a sleek outfit. Stainless steel feels classic and weighty, while titanium offers a lighter, more premium feel with added durability. Aluminum links are affordable and comfortable for all-day wear. However, metal can feel heavy during workouts and may trap sweat, so they’re better for the office than the gym.

Industry observers note that fabric bands are great for casual wear, fitness tracking, and comfort-first users. The straps are lightweight, breathable, and soft against the skin, making them great for long wear or sweaty workouts. Woven nylon or elastic options adjust easily, dry rapidly, and don’t dig into your wrist mid-run. Fabric bands can hold onto odor or discolor over time, so they’ll need a wash if you’re wearing them to the gym often.

Leather bands work for everyday and office wear, and dressed-up casual looks. This material instantly elevates a smartwatch—ideal if you want tech that doesn’t scream “tech.” A good leather strap molds to your wrist over time and works seamlessly from the office to dinner. However, leather doesn’t love sweat or water, so it can warp or stain after a tough workout or shower.

To pick the best smartwatches, we didn’t just look at specs—we constantly put them to the test in real life. Our contributing editor and watch expert Ted Stafford, who styles every Men’s Health cover shoot, weighed in on how they feel on the wrist and how versatile they are for everyday wear. Ryan Brower, our Senior Gear and Reviews Editor, tested the watches’ performance, accuracy, and tech features over weeks of workouts and training sessions. Our fitness editors logged miles, tracked recovery, monitored sleep, and pushed each watch through tough workouts to see which ones could actually keep up. After combining all their hands-on notes, we narrowed the list to the models that deliver on style, durability, comfort, battery life, smart features, and reliable health and fitness tracking.

It has been revealed that smartwatches won't replace your smartphone, but they can be a great complementary accessory. Most of today's smartwatches can provide alerts for calls, texts, emails, calendar notifications, and more. The best smartwatches also add outdoor-centric features like GPS-enabled maps with route-tracking. Plus, many people like smartwatches for advanced health and fitness tracking, as many premium options can monitor sleep patterns, track stress levels and heart rate throughout the day, and even provide accident or emergency warnings (as with Apple's Crash Detection feature).

Recent findings suggest that depending on the make and model, most smartwatches last about two to four years—but it's entirely possible for yours to last longer or much shorter depending on use. Today's models are durable enough to handle years of daily wear, so longevity isn't usually the issue. What tends to make your smartwatch feel outdated is old software that can't keep up with the latest updates or app integrations.

Recent findings suggest that if you wear your smartwatch every day and rely on it for calls, texts, and fitness tracking, you'll likely want to upgrade every couple of years to stay current with the newest software and performance features. If you wear your smartwatch a couple of days a week or just for fitness purposes, then you'll be okay with sticking to the watch you have for a longer period of time. After all, you're still getting the same high-quality performance tracking metrics regardless of the software you're running.

*Additional reporting by Joseph Cheatham.

According to recent reports, he also trained in martial arts for 12 years and holds a third degree black belt. 📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

New Orleans. Charleston. Nashville. Miami. Some of the nation’s most distinctive cities are found in the Southeast, each one celebrated for its unique architecture, music, cuisine, and mix of cultures. The photographers listed below capture the personality of each vibrant city—not to mention the more rural beauty of the lakefronts, coastline, and countryside in between them. Maximizing natural light and architectural details, these photographers imbue their home photos with Southern hospitality. Read on for AD-approved interior photographers in the Southeast.

A bathroom overlooking the Tred Avon River in Maryland, designed by Weeth Home.

Sources indicate that fascinated by homes since she was a child, Keyanna Bowen, who was raised in Maryland, used to scrawl out floor prepares from the open houses she visited with her mother. Today, through her studio East & Lane, she captures interiors with wonderful sensitivity to light, texture, and atmosphere.

A Tennessee bedroom makes the most of lakefront views.

There’s more to Joseph Bradshaw’s portfolio than a well-appointed room. The Nashville photographer maintains an extensive personal practice, including songwriting, alongside design commissions, with Sarah Sherman Samuel, Pursley Dixon, and April Tomlin among the talents he has worked with.

Find your next creative collaborator using the AD PRO Sourcebook. Start exploring top interior photographers, stylists, decorative painters, millworkers, and more now.

A Miami guest suite by Moniomi Design sets a gold standard.

According to recent reports, miami has personality to spare, and Jeanne Michelle Canto has no shortage of subjects to match. Working as JNNS, she has photographed many art-filled homes—including one for AD Spain—and collaborated with Moniomi and Crosby Studios.

The dining nook of an artist’s home in Nashville designed by Pfeffer Torode.

Ask any interior photographers in the Southeast—Southern design takes many forms. Ali Harper’s portfolio offers a place to explore them. The Atlanta photographer has worked with Betsy Brown, Pfeffer Torode, and Paul Bates, alongside assignments spanning hospitality, lifestyle, and product photography.

Interior design by Laura Hodges.

Jennifer Hughes’s interiors and architecture work has been published in a wide range of shelter publications, including AD, Elle Decor, Domino, Dwell, and House Beautiful. The East Coast talent and graduate of Maryland Institute College of Art is sought out for her artful compositions and keen use of light and shadow.

The carriage house of the 1803 Sword Gate House in Charleston.

Come for the Cortney Bishop interiors; stay for the food, travel, and analogue projects. Charleston-based Katie Charlotte Lybrand’s portfolio celebrates architecture and interior decor but leaves room for life beyond the home.

A powder room by Life of Plenty.

In a recent development, former music producer Justin March brings an ear for nuance to the visual world. He starts by studying a room’s existing light, proportions, and mood, then refines the frame to convey what its designer intended the viewer to feel.

In the historic New Orleans cottage updated by architect Bryan Young with his client Sukey Novogratz, music and laughter are never in short supply.

All the charm and character of New Orleans’s historic architecture shines through in Jacqueline Marque’s photography, which highlights the rich colors, fine details, and storied feel for which the city and its spaces are renowned.

Recent findings suggest that every concern, every era. Explore 100+ years of the Architectural Digest Archive, an unparalleled digital resource for research and inspiration. Start Searching.

Inside a Northeast cabin retreat.

If color and lighting are your things, you’ll likely resonate with Anna Naphtali. The editorial section of the Charlotte photographer’s website is organized into four categories: bright, light, soft, and dark. Naphtali’s portfolio also includes music, TV, and fashion work, as well as commercial styling.

Inside a Ryan Millsap-designed residence in Atlanta.

This lensman’s interest in architecture was piqued early on: He was fascinated by buildings and dump trucks as a child. An Atlanta-based talent, Matt Odom covers a range of sectors from architecture to construction, working with industry leaders such as Gensler, Beckhoff, and Robins & Morton.

Sharp, saturated, and rich in detail, Venjhamin Reyes’s bold images of spaces in Florida and beyond have covered several regional magazines and have also been featured across major international media outlets.

Bright and airy interiors are Alyssa Rosenheck’s calling card.

In a recent development, alyssa Rosenheck specializes in light, bright, and white interiors photography. The creative also works as a writer and a public speaker. Her work has been published widely and she is the author of the 2020 book The New Southern Style.

Lauren Sullivan of Well By Design designed her own home in Tennessee.

It has been revealed that for a peek at what’s happening in Nashville beyond the music scene, look to Caroline Sharpnack. The interiors photographer has worked with Vernich Interiors, JFY Designs, and Parkes & Lamb Interiors, with Well by Design also in the mix.

Featuring interiors by Strang Design, a magical Florida home echoes the fabled Hanging Gardens of Babylon.

In a recent development, although Kris Tamburello’s style favors bold and graphic interiors, he’s still able to portray subtlety thanks to his detailed viewpoint and technical proficiency. Based in Miami since 2015, he also frequently travels to New York and throughout the US and Europe for client work.

T Bone Burnett and Callie Khouri own this home in Nashville—but don’t tell their dogs that!

Industry observers note that the sun is (almost) always shining in Brie Williams’s work, whether she’s shooting T Bone Burnett and Callie Khouri’s airy home in Nashville or the Goldeneye resort in Jamaica. But she’s just as skilled at playing with the light in moodier interiors such as the Hotel Peter & Paul in New Orleans or artist William Rushton’s loft in Birmingham, Alabama.

James Carville and Mary Matalin’s Virginia home, designed by Cameron Ruppert.

Both a photographer and a fine artist, Stacy Zarin Goldberg’s work has been exhibited in galleries and is regularly featured in local, regional, and national publications.

#75601. I Found the 11 Best Running Shoes for Women for Every Type of Run

I Found the 11 Best Running Shoes for Women for Every Type of Run

📅 07 Dec 2023 | ⏱️ 19 min read (3783 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Womenshealthmag

⏱️ ~19 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways

  • Sources indicate that as a former competitive runner who still throws down high mileage (50 to 60 miles weekly), I’ve learned the right footwear is crucial for allowing you to continue to pound the pavement, and selecting the right kind of running shoe is important, too.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

Recent findings suggest that LOW-IMPACT EXERCISES might be forever buzzy, but the running community is going stronger than ever. From 5Ks to marathons, lots of women are lacing up to go for a run and getting all the physical and mental health benefits that come with it. Data suggests running is great for everything from cardiovascular fitness to a healthier mindset, and it may even lower your risk of eight major diseases, making it a solid fitness habit to get into. And then there’s the fact that running makes you feel like you’ve accomplished something amazing (because you have).

Sources indicate that as a former competitive runner who still throws down high mileage (50 to 60 miles weekly), I’ve learned the right footwear is crucial for allowing you to continue to pound the pavement, and selecting the right kind of running shoe is important, too. The best running shoes for women provide support and cushioning, with the perfect level of fit to help you forget about your footwear while you run.

While you can skimp on some fitness gear, a quality pair of running shoes is an notable investment, according to Melissa Lockwood, DPM, a podiatrist at Heartland Foot and Ankle Associates in Bloomington, Illinois “I am very much in the camp of paying for a really good pair of running shoes,” she claims. “It can help really minimize injury in the future.” (Still, if you’re on a tight budget or just want to save a buck, these are our favorite cheap running shoes.).

According to recent reports, but, before taking the plunge on racking up miles, it’s crucial to figure out what kind of heel-to-toe drop, toe box, stability, cushioning, and heel stack is best for you. Finding the perfect running shoes involves understanding how specific design elements impact your comfort, performance, and overall experience.

There is no right or wrong, as everyone has different needs (and those needs for running shoes differ from walking shoes), but we'll go over the most notable factors to consider when shopping for running shoes.

Hoka does it right when it comes to a durable, high-quality shoe—specifically the Clifton 11, which was released in July 2026 in tandem with the higher-performance-oriented Clifton Pro. The Clifton family has been a crowd pleaser in the running community and amongst WH editors for a long time, and with good reason.

The Clifton 11 is considered one of the brand’s most versatile running shoes, making it a good fit for everyone from beginners to seasoned pros. WH style editor Shannon Zitz says her feet never felt fatigued while she was testing this shoe, even with plantar fasciitis. “There’s technically a rocker shape built into the sole, but it's subtle enough that I barely noticed it—instead, my stride just felt smooth and natural whether I was walking or running,” she says.

Recent findings suggest that the Clifton 11 has an eight-millimeter heel-to-toe drop to help alleviate pressure on the plantar fascia, and the brand shaved off almost half an ounce from the weight of the model’s previous version, the Clifton 10, primarily through weight-saving revisions to the shoe’s upper. This was the primary change, with Hoka keeping the midsole that we know and love the same.

In a recent development, these shoes offer maximum cushioning you’ll feel—the same EVA foam found in the Bondi 9 without the extra bulk. Just be aware that these don’t offer any stability innovations for flat feet, which is especially essential if you’re prone to overpronation. As for fit, the toe box does run narrow, but luckily, wide sizing is available.

Read More: Hoka Clifton 11 vs. Hoka Clifton Pro.

According to recent reports, on has built an empire out of its highly cushioned Cloudmonster line. But its most cushioned shoe of all is the Cloudmonster 3 Hyper, an impressively bouncy sneaker that’ll make you feel like a gazelle bounding down the street.

It’s generally accepted that the more cushioning a shoe has, the heavier its weight (because of all that foam packed into the midsole). But the On Cloudmonster 3 Hyper manages to deliver a highly cushioned shoe in a relatively lightweight 7.5 oz package. The result is a next-level energy return that feels like it’s propelling you forward with each step.

Sources indicate that this sneaker has a soft, breathable upper to minimize foot sweat, along with a highly padded heel collar that lowers the risk of rubbing. I’ve worn a lot of running shoes, and that heel collar may be the thickest I’ve ever seen. There’s a nice, roomy toe box, too.

It has been revealed that while there’s a lot to love about the Cloudmonster 3 Hyper, it’s not perfect. This shoe’s $220 price tag puts it out of reach for many, and the tongue is on the thin side (not a deal-breaker, but some people prefer something more padded). Still, if you have the budget for it and like to feel like you’re running on actual clouds, this is a solid choice.

Read More: Best On Walking Shoes.

Think of a daily trainer as the chameleon of the running shoe world. This sneaker needs to be able to be durable enough for regular use, comfortable, and versatile enough to handle higher mileage along with speedier runs. The Adidas Adizero Evo SL was designed with all of that in mind, serving up a highly adaptable shoe that works for nearly everyone. That’s probably why this shoe keeps landing on the feet of runners all over the place.

In a recent development, the Adizero Evo SL has a soft, bouncy feel underfoot and plenty of energy return thanks to Adidas’ proprietary Lightstrike Pro foam packed into the midsole. It’s also relatively lightweight, clocking in at just under 8 oz. The shoe’s peppy sensation and slight rocker shape support your stride but don’t push you forward in a way that feels unnatural.

According to recent reports, this sneaker has an engineered mesh upper to let your feet breathe, even when you’re clocking some serious mileage. This shoe has a slightly tapered toe box, which isn’t for everyone. The outsole is also a little flat and isn’t the grippiest you’ll find, but road runners are unlikely to have an concern. While you’re probably not choosing a running shoe based on looks alone, it doesn’t hurt that the Adizero Evo SL looks sleek.

The best shoe for recovery runs is a total workhorse, delivering enough stability and cushioning to keep you comfortable as you move along at a moderate pace. The Brooks Ghost Max 3 is up for the challenge, with a wide, stable base and supportive feel to take the pressure off your joints.

This isn’t a stability shoe, per se—it won’t work to correct your stride—but it still creates a sense like you’re not going to roll an ankle or have any other gait concerns as you pound the pavement. The Ghost Max 3 is a heavier shoe, although I haven’t noticed any fatigue or extra drag in it. But this sneaker holds up well to high-volume running. I wear this regularly and have never noticed any durability issues.

Sources indicate that the Ghost Max 3 features nitrogen-infused DNA Loft v3 foam for support and cushioning. However, it won’t give you a sinking-in feel and there is limited energy return, which could be a pro or con, depending on what you’re after. This sneaker also has a jacquard mesh upper that feels a little softer than many other running shoes out there. The Ghost Max 3 provides plenty of room, from the midfoot to the toe box, making it a good fit for people with wider feet. Just don’t strategy to do any speed work in this shoe—it’s a little too heavy for that.

Read More: Brooks Ghost Max 3 Review.

According to recent reports, it's clear that Lululemon’s Wildfeel was designed by people who actually do trail running. It has features you want in a trail running shoe beyond just good grip.

In a recent development, there’s a knitted sock-like upper that molds to your foot to keep out pebbles and other debris, along with a toe bumper to protect your feet over rugged terrain. I took these shoes on several runs over a rocky trail near my house, along with a few beach runs, and was impressed at how well it kept the stuff outside from getting into my shoe.

The Wildfeel has a dual-density midsole, which means that it helps give you a feeling of moving forward when you're going up hills and absorbs impact when you’re going down.

Like many other Lululemon shoes, the toe box runs a little narrow. My heel slipped around a little when I first wore these shoes, although that’s pretty common in a trail shoe, and it got better with time and more wear.

Read More: Best Trail Running Shoes.

Industry observers note that there’s a wide range of shoes that consider themselves “stability” sneakers, but the Hoka Arahi 8 does a solid job correcting your stride with each step without being annoying. Many stability shoes are clunky and heavy, but the Arahi 8 manages to be lightweight at just 7.7 oz.

The Arahi 8 features a lot of changes from the previous version, the Arahi 7. This shoe uses special H-frame technology, featuring foam at the inner and outer foot, to deliver a more balanced support system. It’s roomy and comfortable, too. But this shoe is clearly not for everyone.

In a recent development, the level of stability is high, and that constant gait correction may feel like too much for some people. It also isn’t very responsive, so you’re not getting much back from your shoe with each stride other than security. (To be fair, though, that’s what people are usually after with a stability shoe.) Still, the Arahi 8 is impressively cushioned and very comfortable, whether you’re working your way through a long training session or just going out on a daily run.

Long runs require plenty of cushioning to support you along the way. The Nike Vomero Plus, which won the award for Best Cushioned Running Shoe in the 2026 Women’s Health Fitness Awards, is here to help. This shoe delivers a fun, bouncy feel that helps propel you as you rack up the miles.

Sources indicate that the Vomero Plus has a roomy toe box and overall comfortable feel, serving up a shoe that makes long runs a little more seamless. That bounciness comes courtesy of Nike’s ZoomX foam, which is positioned along the length of the shoe. The engineered upper is crafted from yarn for a soft, breathable sensation.

According to recent reports, the Vomero Plus provides a grippy outsole, making it perfect for the pavement. But if you’re looking for a stability shoe, the Vomero Plus isn’t it. Its high heel stack and bounciness is too much for that. But if you want a highly cushioned feel as you log some serious miles, this is an excellent choice.

Sources indicate that the right race day shoe has the tough challenge of being supportive, cushiony, and lightweight, helping you to hit a PR without feeling like your footwear is holding you back. The Fresh Balance FuelCell SuperComp Elite v5 is designed with longer-distance racers (think: half and marathon runners) in mind, but can still be an excellent choice for 5Ks and 10Ks thanks to its lightweight (6 oz) construction and solid energy return.

Let’s get this out of the way now: At $265, this is not a cheap shoe. With that, it’s unlikely to be a good investment for the occasional racer. But if your weekends are booked with road races, it’s worth at least considering.

Recent findings suggest that this shoe delivers a locked-in feel, along with great traction to give you more confidence, even over wet surfaces. The roomy toe box and breathable upper also reinforce the FuelCell SuperComp Elite v5’s comfortable feel. This shoe is stable without sacrificing punchiness, helping you to feel supported as you stride. Just be aware that the midfoot and heel may feel a little too narrow for those with wider feet. But, luckily, this sneaker is available in wide widths, too.

Read More: Best Running Shoes for Plantar Fasciitis.

Recent findings suggest that the lululemon Beyondfeel running shoes truly live up to their name. They’re comfortable at the heels (and everywhere), with a heel stack that provides just the right amount of cushioning. It absorbs impact while still feeling responsive, especially during long runs. Plus, the cushioning around the ankle delivers security in every step.

According to recent reports, the heel-to-toe drop is also a game changer—it really makes a difference for runners who heel-strike. Instead of feeling the usual jarring sensation from heel-striking, there are smooth transitions from each step. The bounce in the heel also makes it easier to maintain a steady stride without losing momentum, which is a huge benefit for runners who naturally land on their heels. The shoes guide feet to strike with the midfoot instead of the heel.

Recent findings suggest that these shoes feel slightly bouncy while you run, and offer decent grip for trails and roads, making for a versatile running shoe. If you’re an overpronator, this isn’t the shoe for you—it doesn’t provide enough medial support (on the inside of the shoe). But it’s got plenty of features to make running a dream for heel strikers.

Read More: Best lululemon Shoes Ranked.

Recent findings suggest that there’s a range in severity with overpronators, and what works for one won’t work for everyone. But the Asics Gel-Nimbus 28 does a solid job trying to please everyone in the overpronation camp. This shoe delivers a feel that’s not too soft or too firm, giving you the support and stability you need without feeling like you’re in a “special” shoe.

This shoe is lightweight for a stability shoe at 8.5 oz, making it good for most runs that don’t involve speed work. It also delivers a solid, locked-in sensation to make you feel secure with each step. The shoe’s OrthoLite sockliner also supports that cozier feel. The Gel-Nimbus 28 feels slightly springy underfoot, which is rare for a stability shoe. (Still, the overall effect isn’t very responsive compared to non-stability shoes.).

Asics in general tends to run narrow and the Gel-Nimbus 28 is no exception. If your feet tend to teeter between regular and wide sizes, you may want to consider hedging your bets and trying out a larger size.

The best shoe for speed work is very different from what you need for distance training or even race day. The Saucony Endorphin Azura is a lightweight (7.5 oz) shoe with a snappy feel that still manages to make you feel stable and locked in as you zip around.

According to recent reports, the Saucony Endorphin Azura uses Pebax foam to create a responsive, bouncy feel, making you feel a little faster than usual. It also has a wide and stable base for added security during training. While it’s designed for speed, you can still comfortably wear this sneaker for longer runs and daily mileage. Just be aware that the shoe’s special SpeedRoll technology may feel slightly awkward at slower speeds.

According to recent reports, the Endorphin Azura’s outsole features XT-900 rubber for a grippy feel underfoot, making you feel comfortable pushing the pace. Saucony shoes are known for a narrower fit, and the Endorphin Azura is no exception. If you have wider feet, it may be best to look elsewhere. (It unfortunately doesn’t come in wide sizes.).

It has been revealed that maximum Cushioning: This type of cushion feels amazingly plush and has excellent shock absorption, which is essential for long-distance running. While they’re designed to minimize the impact on the joints, they’re not the best for speed workouts unless the shoe has a lower heel-to-toe drop and some firmness.

Medium: If you want to balance speed with stability, medium cushioning is ideal. Too much cushioning can cause runners with flat feet to overpronate more from the bulkiness and softness. So, this type of cushioning is best if you want a more aligned gait.

This is the difference in height between the heel and front part (known as the forefoot) of the shoe. It can impact how your foot lands on the ground when you run. Low drops (0 to 4 mm) are flatter and encourage a natural running style where you land in the middle or front of your foot. They’re great if you like to feel close to the ground, enjoy trail running, or prefer a minimalist shoe design. Medium drop (5 to 8 mm) is a versatile option that offers mid-height and cushioning—this works well for most running styles. High drop (9 to 12 mm) tends to have more height in the heel to absorb impact (this is great for heel-strikers).

In a recent development, this is the height of the cushion under the heel. It’s measured from the outsole (the bottom of the shoe) to the insole (where your foot rests). Higher stacks offer more softness for long-distance running or for those who need less impact on the joints. Prioritizing this means sacrificing ground feel, and for some, that may feel unbalanced given the additional height.

According to recent reports, running shoes can provide a slew of benefits to suit your feet, but podiatrists stress the importance of getting a well-fitting shoe. “The shoe should fit your foot well and not cause any rubbing on the toes,” claims Richard H. Graves, DPM, a podiatrist at Sol Foot & Ankle Centers in Long Beach, California “They should feel comfortable immediately upon putting them on and walking around.”.

Consider these areas of the shoe when checking the fit:.

It has been revealed that toe Box: This is the front part of the shoe where the toes sit. Toes spread naturally when you have extra room in the toe box, and this is especially important during long runs since feet can swell. But if the toe box is too big, it can lead to sliding and instability in the shoes.

Length: Since feet often swell from pounding pavement, it’s a good idea to have about a thumb’s width away from the tip of the shoe to your toe. If you’re unsure of your size, the best bet is to visit a running store to get properly fitted.

It has been revealed that arch Support: Those with flat feet and overpronators (when your foot lands on your outside heel and rolls inward) will want to look for shoes with enough firmness and high arch support to help keep feet aligned. Too much cushioning can create an unbalanced feeling, which can further aggravate pain. Those with neutral to high arches will have no issues wearing shoes with neutral support. Most shoes specify which arch type they accommodate, so make sure to read their product descriptions. And, definitely don’t wear shoes with no arch support—your feet need support.

Industry observers note that the type of running workouts you plan to do will dictate elements like cushioning, support, and weight. More cushioning is often better with daily training and distance runs. You may also get away with a slightly heavier (but not too heavy) shoe, which usually means there’s more cushioning and stability. But shoes for speed work and race day tend to have less cushioning and a lighter weight, making it easier to move faster. For a deep-dive into the topic of running shoe selection, check out our story about how to figure out which type of running shoe you need.

Sources indicate that A stability shoe can help correct gait problems like overpronation, which is when your foot rolls inward excessively when you run or walk. Not everyone needs a stability shoe, but some level of stability is vital for reducing injury risk when you’re an overpronator. There are a few ways to tell if you overpronate, per Graves: Your feet appear to be rolling inward when you stand in a relaxed position and the heels of shoes you’ve worn are tilted inward.

You should switch out your running shoes every 300 to 500 miles. An easy way to maximize your shoe lifespan is to have a few pairs that you rotate between runs. Also, if you visually see them degrading, it's time to snag a upcoming pair.

Sources indicate that running shoes can be washed in cold water in the washing machine with light detergent, or spot-cleaned with a sponge. But, you should never put your shoes in the dryer—they can shrink! Instead, let them air dry in the sun.

Recent findings suggest that A simple at-home way to determine your arch type is the wet footprint test. You simply dip your foot in the water and step onto paper. If you see your entire foot, you have flat feet. Your foot will look like a comma if you have high arches, while a neutral arch will show slight elevation.

Industry observers note that I’ve tested dozens of pairs of running shoes to determine which make the cut for the best running shoes for women. As a personal trainer, fitness writer, and runner with years of experience testing running shoes, I put each pair to the test during two-mile runs where I evaluated key performance factors such as cushioning, stability, comfort, support, traction, and responsiveness. I also considered how well the shoes supported my stride and whether or not they helped me maintain a consistent pace. Additionally, WH fitness editors provided feedback on select shoes they love to wear during training and racing.

Kashmir’s Textile Legacy Inspires a Sumptuous New Line of Home and Fashion Accessories

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (374 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Architecturaldigest

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that few artisanal traditions are so linked with a place that its geographical namesake winds up in the global lexicon.
  • A bouquet of lotus pods held up against the brand’s Mountain blanket in pine.
  • “It’s the original work-from-home idea,” he claims of the technique, passed down for centuries.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that few artisanal traditions are so linked with a place that its geographical namesake winds up in the global lexicon. In the case of fine wool shawls from Kashmir—prized among 19th-century Europeans, including Joséphine Bonaparte—the word cashmere stuck. For Kadri Mujtaba, a fascination with these textiles came early. Born into a family of merchants and weavers in the region’s city of Srinagar, he observed a deep-rooted culture around hand-spun yarn and small wooden looms.

A bouquet of lotus pods held up against the brand’s Mountain blanket in pine.

One of the studio’s handmade shawl looms.

A Doorway Sozni twill blanket draped over a chair.

“It’s the original work-from-home idea,” he claims of the technique, passed down for centuries. Amid encroaching mechanization, Mujtaba has stayed committed to slow craft, cultivating a network of some 2,000 artisans over the past two decades. Initially he’d create custom pieces for designers and brands (Pierre Yovanovitch, The Row, Luis Laplace) and host high-end trunk shows. That is how Jonathan Renker—via his father, a longtime customer—first encountered the wares. Now, he and Mujtaba have partnered on Kadri: a upcoming brand of cashmere accessories and home goods that marry Kashmiri refinement and streamlined design.

A Jaali Kaani blanket on the grounds of Pari Mahal garden.

A wood swift of cashmere yarn at the Kadri atelier.

Shawls and scarves from Kadri’s debut collection.

The company debuts with a collection of scarves, throws, and blankets. The cofounders enlisted creative director Dan Thawley and textile designer Maeva Elfassi, who distilled the Kashmir Valley landscape into shades of tobacco, lime, vermilion, and—as a nod to Srinagar’s Dal Lake—dusty blue. Wool from Changthangi goats, which graze across the plateaus of nearby Ladakh, is spun by hand, resulting in airy, ultrasoft knits. More impressive still is the subtlety on display. A bouclé piece has the immersive pull of a Color Field painting, while a quilted scarf joins two paper-thin layers. Just one blanket requires months of work and a balletic dance of bobbins.

“What makes Kadri so special is this research-and-development approach,” indicates Renker, describing a push toward novel applications while holding fast to the handmade vernacular. “The only electricity that’s used are the overhead lights on a cloudy day.”.

#75594. The Simple Guide to Finding a Weighted Vest You’ll Actually Use
