Why Better Recovery Might Be the Missing Link in Your Workout Routine

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1775 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Womenshealthmag

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in.
  • It has been revealed that you work hard in the gym, nail your nutrition, and consistently try to challenge yourself with heavier weights or more reps.
  • It has been revealed that A plateau can be incredibly frustrating, but there is some good news: It may not be your meticulously planned workouts that need tweaking.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

It has been revealed that you work hard in the gym, nail your nutrition, and consistently try to challenge yourself with heavier weights or more reps. But no matter what you do lately, it seems as if your progress just won’t budge. So what’s going on?

It has been revealed that A plateau can be incredibly frustrating, but there is some good news: It may not be your meticulously planned workouts that need tweaking. The solution for your stall in progress may lie in something a little simpler: recovery.

According to recent reports, many people think results happen during our sweat sessions, but in actuality, the gains we’re working toward happen afterward. Adapting to stress, building muscle, and getting stronger all happen when we take rest. So, before you fire your personal trainer or scour the internet for a newly introduced workout strategy, try making a few simple tweaks to how you spend your downtime, if you’re even giving yourself any.

Read on for what the science and experts say about recovery—and how you can use yours to escape your fitness plateau.

Meet the experts: Donna Duffy, PhD, is an associate professor in the department of kinesiology at the University of North Carolina, Greensboro, and head of research at Collective X Health, a women's health intelligence and research platform co-founded by WH advisory board member Stacy Sims. Lisa Woodroffe, MD, is a sports medicine physician at the University of Iowa Health Care and team doctor for several of the Iowa Hawkeye women’s athletic teams. Asad Siddiqi, DO, is the chief of rehabilitation medicine at NewYork-Presbyterian Brooklyn Methodist Hospital.

Working out is only one piece of the equation when it comes to seeing results. In order to get all the benefits of training, your body needs time to rest and recover after a workout. “During rest, your body recovers using sleep, food, and downtime to repair the tissues you’ve stressed during training and prepare them to handle the next challenge,” claims Donna Duffy, PhD, an associate professor in the department of kinesiology at the University of North Carolina, Greensboro.

In a recent development, there’s a lot that goes on in your body during rest: In addition to your muscles repairing and building back stronger, you experience a nervous system reset—as your heart rate decreases after a training session, your body shifts out of a stressed state and begins to calm down, Duffy explains. Then there is increased blood flow during and after exercise, which helps flush out things like lactic acid and delivers fresh oxygen and nutrients to stressed parts of the body.

That is, assuming you’re giving your body enough time to do all that. “If you continually pile more workouts on top of fatigue without giving your body enough time and resources to recover, that fatigue can start to interfere with your overall performance in and out of the gym,” Duffy says.

Recent findings suggest that when a person fails to recover adequately, a weight that seemed doable on Monday feels heavier on Wednesday, and an easy run becomes a hard one. All of this can be incredibly frustrating, and may make people think they just need to work harder, but experts say sometimes the opposite is true. “Your body may not need more training,” states Duffy. “Instead, it may need more opportunity to recover from the training you're already doing.”.

It has been revealed that your body may be sending you signals that you’re not as well recovered as you think. According to Duffy, some common signs that your body has not recovered well include:.

Showing signs of poor recovery? Start by making these tweaks.

In a recent development, when deciding if your body needs a rest, consider factors like workout duration, intensity, and fatigue, indicates Asad Siddiqi, DO, chief of rehabilitation medicine at NewYork-Presbyterian Brooklyn Methodist Hospital. Soreness or fatigue that stays below a 3 to 4 out of 10 during or immediately after training and does not last beyond 24 to 36 hours is the upper limit of “acceptable” exercise-induced discomfort, and a day in between loading is probably fine. Meanwhile, if you go above a 5, Dr. Siddiqi recommends taking an extra day beyond that to monitor how you’re recovering before doing the same workout again. Typically, a two-day break will allow people enough time to recover, but the most vital barometer is how you feel, he says. If you’re still super sore and think your form will be compromised, you need more time off.

Bob and Brad A7 Pro Massage Gun with Heat and Cold Therapy.

TriggerPoint Grid Multi-Density Foam Roller.

Recent findings suggest that this doesn’t mean you need to be completely inactive during those days off, particularly if you’re doing circuit training. If you hit arms really hard on Monday and need to give them some extra time to recover, you can still do legs the next day. But, if you are doing intense and fatiguing full-body workouts, try alternating resistance training with low-impact aerobic or mobility exercises like yoga.

Even if you’re doing circuit training, at a minimum, most people should have at least one full rest day per week, says Lisa Woodroffe, MD, a sports medicine physician at the University of Iowa Health Care and team doctor for several of the Iowa Hawkeye women’s athletic teams. And, if you’re someone who has been feeling consistently sore, unusually fatigued, or seeing a dip in performance, it’s time to up your number of rest days.

Recent findings suggest that for a variety of reasons, many active people are just simply not eating enough, claims Dr. Woodroffe. “They are either underestimating how much energy they are expending in exercise, or overestimating what they are eating, or with busy schedules running out of time in their day to get everything they need.” It’s also worth mentioning that some people may be exercising with the explicit goal of losing weight—which can result in underfueling for their workouts, she says.

In a recent development, eating enough is critical for recovery. “We know that insufficient fueling patterns have cascading and multiplying effects on the body’s ability to respond to training load and recovery,” Dr. Woodroffe indicates. “All cells of the body need adequate energy to maintain optimal function. When there is not enough energy to go around, there will be effects not only at the cellular level but eventually also at the organ system level.” We’re talking effects on muscle recovery, bone density, cardiovascular function, and cognitive performance.

That’s why experts recommend having a plan in place for getting all the fuel you need. “Emphasizing a routine of three to five meals a day that includes carbs for energy, protein for muscle building, and fresh vegetables and fruits for minerals and gut health is the baseline,” says Dr. Siddiqi. You don’t need to count calories if that’s not your thing—but you should have a goal of at least three meals supplemented by additional snacks every day that hit all of the macros (carbs, protein, and fats).

Sources indicate that protein is particularly important for active people, but no macro should be ignored. Dr. Woodroffe always notes that no food groups should be restricted unless otherwise directed by a medical professional. If you need any help with your fueling strategy, it’s a good idea to check in with a doctor or dietitian who can give you personalized recommendations.

One overall, simple way to make sure you’re eating enough? Feeling full. You should eat to be satiated and not feel constantly hungry. When it comes to snacking, it’s recommended that you eat easily digestible carbs (Think: fruit, bagels, toast) 30 to 60 minutes before a workout, and then a combination of carbs, protein, and fluids within 60 minutes following. It’s one reason dietitians love chocolate milk as a post-workout drink.

Your training program is a balancing act. “A plateau can happen either due to not enough training, or not enough recovery,” Dr. Woodroffe notes. But how can we actually tell which one is happening? What are the clues that someone needs to pull back versus increase the challenge?

“Overall, training should be a positive experience that challenges the body and mind but doesn’t put you out of commission,” Dr. Siddiqi claims. You want to be sore after a workout, but not so much that you can’t move. If you’re experiencing the symptoms above that are signs you’re not recovering properly, you’re probably overloading and should pull back. Start by taking two full rest days to give your body a real chance to recover, and then consider implementing one additional rest day per week compared to your old schedule or adjusting your training strategy to allow for less intensity.

On the flip side, if you’re plateauing and not feeling drained at all, then it may be because you need to challenge yourself more. If that’s the case, Dr. Siddiqi recommends a steady increase in load by roughly 10 percent week over week. “The definition of ‘load’ in this situation is variable, and so this could mean 10 percent more intense based on your perceived exertion, 10 percent greater distance, 10 percent greater duration, or however else you think could be meaningful,” he states. The key, though, is to have a steady increase on your way to your goal, avoiding any major spikes.

So how do you know when symptoms are more than just poor recovery after a challenging workout versus a health problem that needs a professional follow-up? “Sometimes fatigue, soreness, or a dip in performance really can be a sign that you need more recovery, but it's also crucial not to assume that every change is caused by your training,” notes Duffy. “If symptoms are persistent, getting worse, or affecting your ability to function normally, there may be something else going on.”.

Duffy suggests seeing a health care professional if:.

Whatever you may be experiencing—a regular old case of doing too much or something more serious—consider this your sign to take a second, check in with yourself, and don’t hesitate to ask for support. You’ll be out there moving again (and even better) before you know it.

Volkswagen is delaying another EV based on the SSP

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (637 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Electrek

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • After delaying development of the long-awaited electric Golf, Volkswagen is delaying another EV based on its SSP platform.
  • As it scrambles to cut costs, Volkswagen brand CEO Thomas Schäfer revealed in an internal memo at the end of October that development of the all-electric Golf is being delayed at its Wolfsburg plant in Germany.
  • The news comes after the VW Group posted an operating loss of €5.9 billion ($6.5 billion) in the third quarter, its largest quarterly loss since the infamous Dieselgate scandal in 2015.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

After delaying development of the long-awaited electric Golf, Volkswagen is delaying another EV based on its SSP platform.

As it scrambles to cut costs, Volkswagen brand CEO Thomas Schäfer revealed in an internal memo at the end of October that development of the all-electric Golf is being delayed at its Wolfsburg plant in Germany.

The news comes after the VW Group posted an operating loss of €5.9 billion ($6.5 billion) in the third quarter, its largest quarterly loss since the infamous Dieselgate scandal in 2015.

“We simply can’t afford this work right now,” Schäfer remarked in the memo reviewed by Reuters. The Wolfsburg plant, AKA the “heart of the VW brand,” is about €300 million ($334.5 million) short of its cost-cutting targets, the memo said.

Volkswagen initially planned to launch the Golf EV in 2028, but Schäfer announced earlier this year that the long-awaited electric car was delayed until closer to 2030.

Schäfer suggested the delay was because the SSP (Scalable Systems Platform), which is being developed through its partnership with Rivian, was taking longer than expected, again due to costs.

According to Autocar, Volkswagen is now delaying the Audi A4 E-tron as well, another vehicle that was initially planned to be among the first based on the SSP platform.

Production of the electric A4 is being pushed back until at least 2029, a year later than originally planned. While the delay is disappointing for Audi fans (including myself) still waiting for an electric A4, it also puts Audi behind rival luxury brands in the mid-size sedan segment.

BMW has the new i3, and Mercedes-Benz has the C-Class EV, both of which feature major improvements in range, charging, and efficiency over their previous-generation EVs.

Volkswagen noted in 2023 that the 800V SSP will serve as a “single future backbone with integrated electric and electronics architecture,” claiming that more than 40 million models were expected to be built on it.

The company also noted investment and R&D costs were expected to be reduced by about 30% compared to the current MEB platform, enabling most models “to achieve the same margin compared to their conventionally powered counterparts.”.

Volkswagen’s software struggles started in its internal division, Cariad, leading to delays, missed targets, and budget overruns.

To fix it, VW turned to Rivian, forming a joint venture to develop its next-gen software-defined vehicle (SDV) electrical architecture.

In March, VW stated several test vehicles, including the ID.EVERY1, Audi, and Scout with the SDV architecture underwent “comprehensive evaluation,” and successfully validated over-the-air (OTA) functionality.

Being cash efficient is good, but delays to the next-gen platform that will keep you competitive with rival brands seem like a problem.

It has been revealed that however, the Audi A4 E-tron delay is not entirely about software. The Autocar report claims Audi demanded significant changes to the SSP platform for the A4 E-tron so it more closely matched the current gas version.

Audi reportedly wanted individual footwells for front and rear passengers, which would require repositioning the battery.

The luxury brand also reportedly asked for a 48V electrical system instead of the traditional 12V setup initially planned.

While development of the Golf EV is on hold, VW’s works council mentioned the pause will not delay its launch, promising to make up for lost time. It’s still expected to launch in 2030. The Audi A4 E-tron is now expected to arrive around 2029.

Latest Update: I Tried Adding 10 Minutes of Daily Mobility to My Routine for Two Weeks. Here’s How My Body—And Mind—Changed

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1625 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Womenshealthmag

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • I’m in my early 30s, which means staying fit requires more of a conscious, consistent effort.
  • Mobility is an incredibly underrated training modality, yet it’s an essential part of healthy aging—especially for those like me who spend most of the day sitting at a desk.
  • This style of movement helps you perform nearly every daily task, from climbing stairs and getting up from a seated position to walking with a full stride and turning your head while driving.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I’m in my early 30s, which means staying fit requires more of a conscious, consistent effort. The natural loss of lean muscle mass and skin elasticity that occurs at this stage of life makes me more mindful of my body and overall well-being. So, I’ve declared this my year of wellness. As part of it, I have been working on adding small bouts of movement that manageably fit into my daily life. Mobility work felt like one of the best ways to do that.

Mobility is an incredibly underrated training modality, yet it’s an essential part of healthy aging—especially for those like me who spend most of the day sitting at a desk. Mobility training focuses on controlled, active movement through a joint’s full range of motion, says Matthew Cifelli, PT, DPT, CSCS, of Attain Physical Therapy.

This style of movement helps you perform nearly every daily task, from climbing stairs and getting up from a seated position to walking with a full stride and turning your head while driving. But as you age or spend extended periods of time being sedentary, it’s common for muscles to tighten, joints to stiffen, and movement to become less efficient.

Industry observers note that “Limited mobility forces the body to compensate with inefficient patterns, increasing the risk of pain, balance problems, and injury,” says Cifelli. Maintaining mobility, on the other hand, “supports independence, joint health, and the ability to move confidently through life.”.

Industry observers note that that’s why I recently decided to add just 10 minutes of mobility work to my daily routine for two weeks. Here’s exactly what I did—and how my body changed.

Mobility is “not just about ‘feeling loose,’” claims Cifelli. “It's about teaching the body to use its flexibility in real movement.” It’s a mix of static stretching and flexibility work that focuses on muscle length. “Mobility training targets how well a joint moves and how well you control that motion, which requires coordinated muscle activation and joint stability.”.

Recent findings suggest that and just a few minutes a day of mobility work can help boost circulation, lubricate the joints, alleviate muscle tension, and improve confidence in daily movement. “Even short sessions, when done daily, create meaningful cumulative change,” he indicates.

My routine included a combination of exercises and hold times I learned from Portia Page, CPT, in addition to a couple of stretches my physical therapist recommended incorporating into my home regimen. I performed each exercise for one minute, one time through.

It has been revealed that during the first week of my experiment, I eased into my 10-minute mobility routine. I was eager to see how it could help improve my “desk body,” a.k.a. tight hips, tense hamstrings, and lower back and neck tension.

I did the workout every morning around 8 a.m. before diving into the madness of the day. It was pretty seamless to add to my mornings, since I have a dedicated workout space in my home, though the routine doesn’t require much space or equipment. Plus, I’m someone who craves routine. Sticking to the same time each morning made this fitness habit sustainable.

From the get-go, it was clear my body was tense and in desperate need of some stretching and mobility work. My legs, back, and hips all felt stiff at the beginning of the workout. Certain exercises, like the standing forward fold, hip flexor stretch, and supine figure-four stretch were more challenging than the rest. For example, during the first week, I found it difficult to touch the floor when doing the forward fold, so I didn’t force it.

By the end of each session, my body was definitely a bit more relaxed, but I knew I needed to stick with mobility work for more than just a week or two in order to achieve meaningful, lasting results.

I was a dancer growing up, and my body was much more flexible then than it is now. While the Pilates classes I attend three to four times a week have definitely helped me stretch and strengthen my body, a dedicated mobility routine felt like exactly what the doctor ordered. I didn’t realize it would help me in my classes, too. By the end of week one, I felt I was able to move through a more seamless range of motion in certain Pilates exercises like the mermaid and the straight-back hinge on the short box.

It has been revealed that heading into week two, I found myself looking forward to my morning mobility session. It started to feel like more of a natural segue into my day, similar to brushing my teeth, taking my vitamins, or getting dressed. Once I wrapped up stretching and sat down at my desk, my body felt more limber and relaxed as I started work. However, after a couple hours of sitting, I felt much more tense again. The experiment taught me to be mindful of that: My body needs movement throughout the day—not just first thing in the morning.

It has been revealed that I felt inspired by this healthy mobility habit and how great I feel afterward, so I wanted to keep the momentum going. During week two, I started building other healthy habits, like getting up to walk around my kitchen and living room every hour and going on a longer brisk walk at the end of the day. Both helped me stay limber throughout the day, rather than just in the morning. My hope is that, with all of these bouts of movement combined, sitting won’t undo all of the wonderful benefits I get from my stretching routine.

By the end of the second week, I was pleased that my body felt more accustomed to the dedicated mobility work than it had during week one. The more challenging stretches also became slightly easier, which made me feel like I was making genuine progress.

The routine became a no-brainer—a staple, if you will—in my morning routine: I’d wake up, brew a soothing latte, and get to work on my yoga mat. It also sparked the desire to get up and move more during the workday rather than remain hunched over my laptop for an extended period of time.

Industry observers note that because I experienced the tension-relieving benefits of this mobility work almost immediately after each session during week two, I’m now inspired to do it at both the start and end of my day. It’s a great way to ease any built-up stiffness after a long day at my desk before slipping into bed.

That said, one thing I’d love to continue working on is my posture. I didn’t experience any groundbreaking improvements during this two-week timeframe, but I’m hopeful that I’ll make progress down the line. I’m also curious to see whether being consistent with this mobility routine long-term will help my body—especially my hips and lower back—feel less stiff after sitting or lounging for longer periods.

Sources indicate that consistency is key. As with any workout, consistency is essential for success. But alas, it’s something I’ve struggled with over the years. Hectic work weeks filled with deadlines and appointments typically push my fitness to the back burner.

Industry observers note that however, during this two-week test period, I was incredibly determined to carve out 10 minutes each day for my stretching regimen, and I’m so glad I did. Sticking with this fitness habit helped me feel better mentally and physically. My body started to feel more flexible and limber by the end of the two-week period—something I don’t think I would have experienced if I were inconsistent with my efforts.

Try this 15-minute mobility routine.

According to Page, a mere 5 to 10 minutes a day of mobility work can make a noticeable difference over time if you’re consistent with the habit. She recommends thinking of stretching “not as a luxury but as basic maintenance for your body—like brushing your teeth.”.

Kickstarting the day with fitness can promote other healthy habits. Starting the day with mobility work inspired me to follow other healthy habits throughout. After all, I was already off to a solid start and wanted to keep that momentum going strong.

Following each mobility session, I felt accomplished, energized, and ready to tackle the day. I found myself sticking with my regular Pilates workouts, making all-around healthier meal choices, snacking less, and adding brief “movement snacks” to my afternoons to break up the time spent sitting at my desk.

Mobility is a low-barrier starting point for movement. What I love best about this mobility workout? I don’t need to leave the comfort of my home or have access to fancy equipment. I’ve seamlessly incorporated these exercises into my self-care routine, and it just takes 10 minutes of my morning before I dive into work deadlines and commitments.

While there’s always room for improvement—and I’d like to add even more stretches to my routine—I felt incredibly accomplished overall with only a 10-minute routine. I’m hopeful that, by starting now and being consistent with mobility training, I can help prepare my body to tackle everyday tasks with ease. This training can also help me stay mobile, confident, and independent in my adventurous lifestyle for the long term.

#75571. Ultra-Processed Food Intake May Increase Dementia, Stroke Risk

Ultra-Processed Food Intake May Increase Dementia, Stroke Risk

📅 18 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (851 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Healthline

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Healthy adults who eat high levels of ultra-processed foods (UPFs) may be more likely to show signs of damage to the brain that could increase the likelihood of stroke and future memory problems, according to a study published October 15 in JAMA Network Open.
  • According to recent reports, UPFs are often defined using the NOVA classification: These foods typically have 5 or more ingredients and include substances not typically found in culinary preparations.
  • UPFs account for more than 50% of daily energy intake in high-income countries, including the United States, Canada, and the United Kingdom.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Healthy adults who eat high levels of ultra-processed foods (UPFs) may be more likely to show signs of damage to the brain that could increase the likelihood of stroke and future memory problems, according to a study published October 15 in JAMA Network Open.

According to recent reports, UPFs are often defined using the NOVA classification: These foods typically have 5 or more ingredients and include substances not typically found in culinary preparations. This category of foods includes packaged snack foods, sugary cereals, soft drinks, and frozen ready-to-eat meals.

UPFs account for more than 50% of daily energy intake in high-income countries, including the United States, Canada, and the United Kingdom.

Previous research has linked these foods to adverse cardiometabolic outcomes. This fresh study adds to growing evidence linking high UPF intake to adverse health outcomes.

This was a cross-sectional analysis of 8,783 adults between the ages of 35 and 69 without cardiovascular disease. The participants were all enrolled in the Canadian Alliance for Healthy Hearts and Minds (CAHHM) and Prospective Urban and Rural Epidemiology-MIND (PURE-MIND) cohorts.

Sources indicate that the researchers used MRI scans to evaluate the participants’ brains. They also set out to analyze the cross-sectional relationship between UPF consumption, body fat, vascular brain injury (VBI), and cognitive performance.

According to recent reports, they measured the participants’ habitual UPF intake using a food frequency questionnaire. Intake was expressed as servings based on a 2,000-calorie-per-day diet.

UPFs accounted for an average of 25% of participants’ daily diets. For the individuals with the highest intake, this increased to 45% of everything on their plates, compared to 16% for those who ate the least.

The researchers also noted that UPFs were not just an added part of individual diets. These foods appeared to replace whole foods.

Recent findings suggest that among people with the highest UPF intake, fruits, vegetables, grains, and other minimally processed foods accounted for 41% of their daily food intake. Among those with the lowest UPF intake, minimally processed foods made up 68% of their daily intake.

When the researchers compared the highest intake to the lowest, they found that those with a higher intake of UPFs had 1.7% more body fat. They also found that people with a higher UPF intake had higher odds of VBI.

“These findings are concerning, but it is vital to remember that an association does not prove cause and effect,” said Michelle Routhenstein, Preventive Cardiology Dietitian at Entirely Nourished, who wasn’t involved in the study.

“From my perspective as a preventive cardiology dietitian, these findings reinforce the importance of nourishing our blood vessels to support both cardiovascular and brain health.”.

Although researchers found no significant differences in cognitive performance, the signs of vascular brain injury observed in the study have been associated with an increased risk of stroke and cognitive decline.

According to recent reports, these findings suggest a possible link between UPF intake and signs of brain changes. However, participants were only assessed once and weren’t followed over time. This means the researchers were unable to determine whether UPFs directly caused the changes.

“While we can’t conclude from this study that limiting UPFs would improve brain health, we have decades of literature demonstrating that higher intakes of green leafy vegetables, brightly colored fruits, whole grains, and lean protein sources are good for brain health,” stated Suzanne Judd, PhD, Director of the UC College of Medicine’s Center for Public Health, who wasn’t involved in the study.

“So focusing more on what can be brought into the diet rather than what should be eliminated might be a good way to start,” she added.

The preservatives [in UPFs] may have a direct impact on the vascular system, while the loss of antioxidants results in a less robust response to inflammation in the body.

It has been revealed that “Additionally, sugar or salt is often added to make the food a bit tastier so people consume it in higher quantities. Over-consumption of food can lead to weight gain and diabetes, which can negatively impact brain health,” Judd mentioned.

It has been revealed that judd told Healthline that it is virtually impossible to completely avoid UPFs. Even some “health” foods, like protein powder and some yogurts, are considered ultra-processed.

It is more crucial to look at diet overall and emphasize consuming foods as close to their natural state as possible, such as fruits, vegetables, grains, and meats purchased raw or frozen and then cooked at home.

Routhenstein recommended starting simply with one manageable swap rather than trying to overhaul your entire diet.

Industry observers note that she remarked that you should identify an ultra-processed food you eat regularly and consider a more nutrient-rich alternative. It is vital to account for convenience, food preferences, budget, and lifestyle so that the change feels realistic and is sustainable over the long term.

According to recent reports, “I want people to feel empowered, not fearful, when making food choices,” said Routhenstein. “Healthy eating does not mean having to cook everything from scratch. What matters most is building consistent, nourishing habits that support both heart and brain health.”.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • BYD opened pre-orders for the third-generation Tang starting at about $34,000 in China.
  • The third-generation Tang joins the Great Tang, or Da Tang, as it’s called in China in BYD’s expanding flagship SUV lineup.
  • We knew it was coming soon after the fresh model appeared in a regulatory filing in China’s Ministry of Industry and Information Technology (MIIT) last month.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

BYD opened pre-orders for the third-generation Tang starting at about $34,000 in China. This five-seat flagship SUV packs more than you’d expect for the money, with two massive 30-inch-plus screens inside and up to 850 km (528 miles) of CLTC range.

The third-generation Tang joins the Great Tang, or Da Tang, as it’s called in China in BYD’s expanding flagship SUV lineup.

We knew it was coming soon after the fresh model appeared in a regulatory filing in China’s Ministry of Industry and Information Technology (MIIT) last month.

BYD unveiled on Friday that pre-orders for the third-gen Tang are officially open, starting at 225,000 yuan, which is around $34,000.

The “large five-seat flagship SUV,” as BYD calls it, is available in three variants, priced from 225,000 yuan ($34,000), 240,000 yuan ($36,000), and 260,000 yuan ($39,000) with rear- and all-wheel-drive variants.

The two lower-priced variants are both RWD, offering a CLTC range of up to 850 km (528 miles), while the top-spec dual-motor AWD version has up to 770 km (478 miles).

All versions use BYD’s second-generation Blade Batteries and Flash Charging tech, enabling the battery to be charged from 10% to 80% in five minutes, or nine minutes to go from 10% to 97%.

According to recent reports, inside, the five-seat SUV packs a surprising amount of tech and premium extras for the price. The setup features two massive screens: a 35.4″ integrated display and another 30″ panoramic theater screen.

Unlike its predessor, which offered five and six-seat configurations, the third-gen Tang will only be offered as a five-seater.

The five-seat setup opens up interior space for passengers and the third-gen Tang has the largest front trunk (frunk) in its class at 205L, BYD said.

Like many of its newly introduced flagship vehicles, the third-gen Tang is equipped with BYD’s latest tech, including its God’s Eye B driver-assistance system and Disus-A dual-chamber intelligent air suspension body control system.

Other added features include a 22-speaker Dynaudio sound system, intelligent electric all‑wheel drive, a high-speed tire blowout stability system, and its iTAC intelligent torque control system.

Lu Tian, the general manager of BYD’s Dynasty division said third-gen Tang vehicles have arrived at dealerships nationwide.

According to recent reports, why mention "two enormous screens" like they are some markers of a more premium vehicle or represent some value? We don't measure the utility of cars by screen real estate per dollar. It's the other part of the utility that matter: range, driving dynamics, road trip convenience, fit/finish/materials/insulation. Personally, I don't think "enormous screens" are going to age well as an automotive trend.

The Great Tang received over 150,000 preorders by the time it introduced in mid-June, a record for a single BYD model.

Since its official launch, the larger Great Tang (Da Tang) has sold more than 10,000 units for four straight months now.

The Great Tang is on sale in China in pure electric (EV) and plug-in hybrid (PHEV) powertrains. The cheapest EV variant starts at 239,900 yuan ($35,500) a CLTC driving range of 800 km (497 miles). Starting at just 269,900 yuan ($40,000), the Flagship EV version uses a bigger (130.15 kWh) battery, offering a CLTC range of up to 590 miles (950 km).

In a recent development, will BYD’s smaller five-seat SUV draw the same demand? Let us know your thoughts in the comments below.

Tech Report: Get the Women’s Health Beginner Workout Strategy: 4-Week Strength Training and Cardio Program

📅 23 Feb 2023 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1906 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Womenshealthmag

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that it’s not just you—everyone really is starting to work out lately.
  • In a recent development, so, if that’s you, let me officially say welcome to the party.
  • The Women’s Health+ 4-Week Beginner Workout Plan takes the guesswork out of starting your fitness journey.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that it’s not just you—everyone really is starting to work out lately. My feed is full of people hitting the weights for the first time ever or setting major goals like getting their first pull-up. And let me just say: It’s awesome!

In a recent development, so, if that’s you, let me officially say welcome to the party. When you’re starting to work out, it can be hard to sift through all the options and find a program that’s actually accessible for a true beginner (or, someone restarting after quite some time). That is, until now.

The Women’s Health+ 4-Week Beginner Workout Plan takes the guesswork out of starting your fitness journey. This comprehensive program guides you through strength and cardio workouts that only take between 20 and 45 minutes. And, of course, it answers every burning question you could have about starting a fitness routine.

No matter your age or experience, starting an exercise routine has many benefits, says Kristen McParland, CPT, your coach for the next four weeks. Building muscle increases total-body strength; your bones, ligaments, and tendons get healthier; and even your blood pressure and immunity may improve. So lace up those sneakers and we’ll see you at the gym now, too.

Download the WH+ 4-Week Beginner Workout Plan.

According to recent reports, over the next four weeks, you’ll follow a specific initiative each day, focusing either on strength training, optional cardio, active recovery, or rest (more on these, below). Each strength workout includes a warm-up and a cooldown (which you can use on cardio days, too). More info on each below.

Simply follow the instructions of each full-body strength training workout in the Women's Health+ Beginner Workout Plan. You can find detailed how-to instructions for each exercise in the Exercise Guide section of the PDF.

Industry observers note that equipment Needed: Dumbbells, kettlebells, a step or box, and a slam ball. Don’t have access to a kettlebell or slam ball? Don't worry—you can still do those exercises with a dumbbell.

It has been revealed that cardio is important for everyone, regardless of fitness level or routine. That’s because when you’re lifting heavy, your heart needs to be able to take on that stress. Training cardio—through running, cycling, or brisk walking—will help improve your heart strength.

Recent findings suggest that if you’re a beginner when it comes to cardio, simply start at your own pace and build. Complete 20 to 30 minutes of running, biking, cycling, rowing, or using the elliptical or stair climber (whatever you enjoy). No matter which form of cardio you choose, start with interval training: exert yourself for 30 seconds, then go at a light pace for 1 to 2 minutes, alternating the pattern for a total of 20 minutes. The goal is to “get your heart rate up, but then pull it back and recover,” McParland indicates. Eventually, you’ll be able to decrease the rest time and maintain that higher-intensity movement for 15 to 20 minutes without a break.

Your activity on this day is up to you. The goal is to do some kind of low-intensity movement lasting 20 minutes. Some ideas: outdoor walk or hike, bike ride, incline treadmill walk, yoga, or Pilates class.

Take this day to relax so your muscles have time to repair. Still, if your body is craving some type of activity for recovery, you could stretch, go for a walk, or even try a treatment like a massage, sauna, or cold-plunge session.

Here’s how things will progress each week.

Complete the five programmed workouts when it’s convenient for you. Focus on your form and take your two rest days when you need to recover.

Industry observers note that if you completed all the workouts in Week 1, repeat them during Week 2, adjusting one variable in your routine, McParland says: the number of reps or sets, the weight, the speed of the moves (slower is harder). If you missed a workout, don’t stress. Refocus on completing all of the Week 1 workouts before making any of the changes above.

You’ve officially done two full weeks of this workout blueprint—nice job! During this third week, repeat the workouts from Week 2 in exactly the same way or adjust one variable again (reps or sets, weight, range of motion, speed, and rest periods). If you feel you’re crushing it and are ready to level up, try the third full-body strength workout.

Still going strong? Thought so! Hit all six workouts and adjust one variable per workout for an extra challenge (reps or sets, weight, range of motion, speed, rest time). You can also ramp up your cardio time (to 30 to 40 minutes) or speed, shorten rest intervals (for interval training), or raise your step goal by 10 percent (e.g., if your daily step goal was 5,000 a day, make it 5,500).

It has been revealed that ready to become your strongest self? Download the WH+ 4-Week Beginner Workout Plan now.

When you’re just beginning to work out, do a minimum of two full-body strength training days each week, McParland recommends. During both of those days, you should hit at least one exercise from each category of the foundational movement patterns. This will give you enough of a challenge to stimulate muscle growth, she notes.

During the first two weeks of this initiative, you will have two strength training days per week (each session will run 36 to 43 minutes), two optional cardio/step days per week (each session will 20 to 30 minutes), one day of active rest (a stint of low-intensity movement lasting at least 20 minutes), and two recovery days, for a total of five workouts per week.

After those two weeks, see how your body feels and if your body is craving a third day of full-body training. If so, progress to the next phase of this initiative. That weekly schedule consists of three strength training days per week (each session will run 36 to 43 minutes), two optional cardio/step days per week (each session will run 20 to 30 minutes), one active rest day (lasting at least 20 minutes), and one recovery day, for a total of six workouts per week. If your body isn’t ready for three strength-training days yet, wait another two weeks. Once you’ve completed the full four weeks of this plan, consider adding in the third day.

What kind of weights should I choose?

Start with medium weights that will challenge you for 10 to 12 reps, indicates Sariya. Essentially, you’ll want to feel you’ve reached 70 to 80 percent of your rate of perceived exertion (i.e., your fatigue level is at a 7 or 8 out of 10) by the time you’re doing your final reps in a set. When you feel you can do more than 12 reps, it’s time to increase your weight, but keep the same number of reps. This way, you’re always working toward your goal of building strength.

As for how much to increase by: a good rule of thumb is 2.5 to 5 pounds for an upper-body exercise and 5 to 10 pounds for a lower-body move.

What if I need to rest in the middle of a set?

Resting during a workout is important—if you don’t take enough time to recover between exercises, you won’t have enough energy in your body for the next one. With this strategy, you’ll rest between moves in a superset or tri-set for 20 to 30 seconds, or however long it takes to transition between exercises. Between supersets and tri-sets, you’ll rest for one minute.

Industry observers note that if you get fatigued in the middle of a set, push through if you feel safe doing so, Sariya says. However, if you feel dizzy or fear you might drop a weight on yourself, put it down and take time to recover. When you’re feeling better, you can start again. If you’re in any sort of pain, stop the workout entirely.

What kind of cardio should I do?

It has been revealed that cardio is a great supplement to strength training, McParland claims. Plus, it has a slew of benefits, such as better endurance in strength training, better blood pressure regulation, and higher VO2 max, she says.

Recent findings suggest that if you’re a beginner when it comes to cardio, simply start at your own pace and build. Pick any form of cardio you enjoy, whether that’s brisk walking, running, cycling, or swimming, and sprinkle it in two or three days a week for 20 to 30 minutes, McParland recommends.

What should I do on recovery days?

According to recent reports, on an active rest day, you’ll still exercise a bit through low-intensity movement, like a leisurely bike ride or hike. On a recovery day, you’ll do just that: recover. After all, you need to give your muscles time to rebuild and repair, Sariya says. But to maximize the recovery aspect, you can also opt to stretch, go for a gentle walk, or even get a self-care body treatment like a massage.

In a recent development, once you’ve got the WH+ Beginner Workout Proposal under your belt, you’re ready to take things to another level. One way to do that is by simply restarting the program—and completing the moves with heavier weights this time. (This is called progressive overload, and it’s another foundational concept in strength training. The idea is that over time, you will keep increasing the stimulus to your muscles to continuously challenge them and make them stronger.).

Picking the right weight is an art as much as it is a science, but for a general rule of thumb, for upper-body moves, increase your weights by 2.5 to 5 pounds and see how that feels. For lower-body ones, try adding 5 to 10. You should feel like you’re ending each set two to three reps away from failure (where your form starts to break down). You can tell you’re close if your range of motion starts to shorten or your reps are slowing down. That’s how you know you’re successfully challenging yourself. And, if you don’t happen to have a lot of different-sized weights at your disposal, you can always just increase the number of reps you do instead.

But, if you’re looking for something new, WH+ has a bunch of other trainer-created programs to help you grow your knowledge and confidence in the gym and attack other fitness goals.

Volkswagen is getting ready to launch a newly introduced electric car starting at about €20,000 ($22,000) in 2027, and it looks like the entry-level EV may no longer be nameless. A newly filed trademark could have just given away what VW plans to call it.

The fresh entry-level EV is “the last piece of the puzzle,” Volkswagen brand CEO Thomas Schäfer stated last March after unveiling the ID. EVERY1 concept car.

Volkswagen said the production version will launch in 2027 with a starting price of around €20,000 ($22,000).

Industry observers note that the upcoming model will sit below the ID. Polo in Volkswagen’s Electric Urban Car Family, a lineup of compact, affordable electric cars.

According to recent reports, volkswagen’s current entry-level EV lineup includes the ID. Polo, ID. Cross, the Cupra Raval, and Skoda Epiq, all based on its newly introduced MEB+ platform.

According to recent reports, after launching the lower-priced standard versions of the ID. Polo and ID. Cross recently, starting at €24,995 and €27,995, respectively, Volkswagen is preparing to launch an even smaller, more affordable EV next year.

A recent trademark filing with the European Union Intellectual Property Office (EUIPO) and the German DPMA may have just revealed the name of VW’s upcoming €20,000 EV.

Volkswagen filed a trademark application for the name ID. UP on October 22, 2026, with the EUIPO and DPMA, suggesting this will be the name of the upcoming electric car in 2027.

The trademark follows previous reports that VW planned to revive the former Up! name as part of its shift away from its previous numerical naming scheme (ID.3, ID.4, ID.5, etc.).

According to recent reports, volkswagen has kept most details a secret thus far. Like the ID. Polo, the first to go on sale with an established VW nameplate, the ID. UP is expected to use the same 37 kWh LFP battery to reduce costs.

In a recent development, the VW ID. Polo with the 37 kWh battery offers a WLTP range of up to 334 km (207 miles), so the smaller ID. UP will likely provide around the same, if not slightly more.

Industry observers note that volkswagen said it will offer at least 250 km (155 miles) of range. It will also use a latest 70 kW (94 hp) electric motor, enabling a top speed of 130 km/h (80 mph).

The production version of the ID. EVERY1, expected to arrive as the ID. UP, will be one of nine new models VW aims to launch by 2027.

According to recent reports, volkswagen previously noted the entry-level EV will be 3,880 mm long, which would position it between the former Up! (3,600 mm) and the ID. Polo (4,053 mm). Despite its compact size, VW said the electric city car will seat four passengers and offer a luggage compartment volume of 305 liters.

The VW Group’s fresh Electric Urban Car Family is off to a strong start, securing nearly 150,000 orders after series production began in June.

All models within the family are built on the MEB+ platform with a FWD powertrain, and share more than 80% of the components and tech.

According to recent reports, volkswagen said the production version of the ID. EVERY1 will be among the first vehicles based on its zonal, software-defined vehicle (SDV) architecture, which it is developing through its joint venture with Rivian.

In a recent development, alpöge indicates he and Claude encoded their argument in Lean, software used to check mathematical proofs step by step. His note links to 14 downloadable parts of the proof archive, but its availability does not amount to acceptance by the mathematical community.

Industry observers note that alpöge notes he messaged Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei about a possible announcement “late Sunday night,” November 15. He then consulted company leadership and said there was a constraint to respect, without explaining precisely what it was.

“The precise timing is horrible,” he acknowledged. Alpöge rejected a cynical interpretation of the timing, but did not explicitly say the tech giant’s IPO caused the delay.

Anthropic began trading on Nasdaq Thursday, November 19, after raising $81.34 billion in its offering.

Recent findings suggest that some mathematicians fear a “mathocalypse,” with AI solving coveted problems before researchers can learn from pursuing them. Toronto mathematician Daniel Litt warned that, without adaptation, “there’s just no more math in 50 years.” At an MIT panel this week, Buckmaster argued mathematics still requires human understanding.

In a recent development, first posed by Bernhard Riemann in 1859, the hypothesis predicts where certain zeros of the Riemann zeta function fall. The question matters because those zeros are linked to the distribution of prime numbers, whose patterns underlie extensive mathematical research.

A proof would be a historic mathematical result, since experts have been trying to solve that for over a century.

Lean can verify that formal deductions obey its rules. Mathematicians still need to reproduce the archive, check the formalized theorem matches the original conjecture, and examine the claimed result before considering it settled.

Anthropic previously reported progress on the zeta function without claiming to solve the full hypothesis. Alpöge’s new assertion goes far beyond that earlier work.

The Clay Mathematics Institute lists the Riemann hypothesis among its Millennium Prize Problems, each carrying a $1 million award. Under the institute’s prize rules, a proposed solution must be published in a qualifying outlet, survive at least two years of scrutiny, and earn general acceptance before the prize can be considered.

A Handful of Pistachios May Help You Sleep Better, Review Notes

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Could a handful of pistachios before you go to bed really help you sleep better?
  • A review of studies published in Nutrition Research Reviews examines how the nutrients and plant compounds in pistachios might influence sleep health.
  • Pistachios contain several nutrients linked to sleep-related processes, prompting an investigation into whether they might offer benefits beyond their nutritional value.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Could a handful of pistachios before you go to bed really help you sleep better?

A review of studies published in Nutrition Research Reviews examines how the nutrients and plant compounds in pistachios might influence sleep health.

Pistachios contain several nutrients linked to sleep-related processes, prompting an investigation into whether they might offer benefits beyond their nutritional value.

While the findings suggest that pistachios may support sleep, the evidence is inconclusive and warrants further study.

“Pistachios are compelling for sleep research because they bring together several nutrients and plant compounds connected to sleep physiology within one whole food,” stated study author Marie-Pierre St-Onge, PhD, professor of nutritional medicine and director of the Center of Excellence for Sleep & Circadian Research in the Department of Medicine at Columbia University Institute of Nutrition, in a news release.

“Rather than focusing on a single ‘sleep nutrient,’ this review provides a rationale for studying how the complete pistachio food matrix may affect sleep-related pathways,” she continued.

The narrative review examined existing research on pistachios and sleep-related biology.

The researchers explored whether the combination of nutrients in pistachios could promote quality sleep.

Rather than identifying pistachios as a sleep remedy, the researchers outlined biological pathways through which their nutrients and bioactive compounds might influence sleep.

“We were particularly interested in pistachios because they are particularly high in phytomelatonin, polyphenols, and carotenoids, which we noted were plant-derived components that had been shown to have sleep benefits in preclinical studies,” St-Onge told Healthline.

“We also noted their high content of tryptophan and vitamin B6, which are relevant to melatonin production in humans,” she continued.

Pistachios contain several nutrients associated with sleep, including melatonin, which helps regulate the sleep-wake cycle.

Other studies examining the effects of some of these nutrients on sleep offer further context.

According to recent reports, A 2021 systematic review and meta-analysis of tryptophan supplementation found that it may reduce wakefulness after sleep onset, particularly at doses of at least 1 gram (g) daily. However, an ounce of pistachios supplies only about 71 mg, which is much less than the doses examined by the researchers.

Additionally, a 2023 review of dietary polyphenols led by St-Onge identified potential links between plant compounds and sleep outcomes, although results varied across studies.

Neither review established that polyphenols or tryptophan from pistachios specifically affected sleep quality.

“I was not surprised that pistachios may help support sleep, given their combination of nutrients involved in sleep regulation,” said Michelle Routhenstein, MS, a preventive cardiology dietitian at EntirelyNourished, who wasn’t involved in the study.

“Pistachios provide tryptophan, an amino acid the body uses to produce serotonin and melatonin; vitamin B6, which supports these pathways; and magnesium, which plays a role in nervous system function and sleep regulation,” she told Healthline.

The fresh review highlights the concept of the “food matrix,” or how nutrients and bioactive compounds interact within a whole food.

Instead of investigating tryptophan, magnesium, or melatonin individually, researchers were curious about the combined effects of consuming them together in pistachios.

According to recent reports, laboratory and simulated-digestion research offers clues about how fiber and plant compounds in pistachios and peanuts interact with gut microbes. However, these findings do not establish that eating pistachios changes sleep quality in real-world conditions.

Broader nutrition research also points to a relationship between diet and sleep.

A 2021 review in the Annual Review of Nutrition examined evidence linking dietary patterns and individual nutrients to sleep outcomes. The findings suggest a relationship between sleep and diet, but note that more research is needed to determine cause and effect.

In a nutshell, the current evidence builds a compelling case for pistachios as a sleep aid.

However, it’s too soon to recommend pistachios as a sleep remedy, as many factors may affect sleep quality and insomnia.

Industry observers note that “Sleep difficulties can have different underlying causes,” Routhenstein noted. “If inadequate intake of these nutrients is a contributing factor, pistachios may help, but they may not address sleep problems related to other nutrient deficiencies or other causes.”.

Much of the supporting evidence cited in the review comes from studies of individual nutrients, other foods, laboratory experiments, or biological mechanisms rather than from trials involving whole pistachios.

Researchers have also reported significant variations in the melatonin content of pistachios, making the amount in a typical serving difficult to pinpoint.

Recent findings suggest that additionally, the review received support from American Pistachio Growers, and the corresponding author, St-Onge, serves on its advisory board. Larger studies and clinical trials are needed, ideally without industry funding, to ensure well-rounded results.

Indeed, the authors call for randomized controlled trials examining whether eating pistachios affects sleep outcomes, including sleep quality, duration, and melatonin levels.

“This was a review; we noted that the complete profile of pistachios would make them well-suited to support healthful sleep, but research is needed to evaluate this,” St-Onge told Healthline.

According to recent reports, “This is the next step, and something we are actively working on. We also need to better understand what dosage and frequency of consumption would be optimal.”.

Regardless, a handful of pistachios is still considered a healthy choice as part of a balanced diet.

In a recent development, “A small handful, about 1 ounce of shelled pistachios, is an appropriate portion,” Routhenstein noted. “Enjoy them during the day or as a light afternoon or evening snack when you’re hungry.”.

If nutrients like tryptophan help promote sleep, it’s possible that other nuts could yield similar results.

“Other nuts, such as almonds and walnuts, may offer similar benefits because they also contain nutrients involved in sleep regulation,” Routhenstein noted.

“Early research is encouraging, but it’s too soon to say how much they might help.”.

Other foods, like turkey, also contain tryptophan.

It has been revealed that “For someone allergic to nuts, foods such as tofu, beans, oats, eggs, dairy, and fish can provide tryptophan, which the body uses to make serotonin and melatonin,” Routhenstein said. “The goal is to meet their nutrient needs rather than rely on one food to improve sleep.”.

Sleep health depends on multiple factors. As such, Routhenstein recommends a personalized approach to getting better sleep, from what you eat and when you eat to addressing any nutritional gaps.

Sources indicate that “I would also encourage regular, balanced meals throughout the day to support blood sugar management, especially for those with diabetes, while avoiding large meals close to bedtime,” Routhenstein said. “Caffeine later in the day and alcohol in the evening are also worth considering as possible sleep disruptors.”.

Rinnai has launched a fresh lineup of electric heat pump water heaters that adds wifi controls and more installation options to an appliance that can cut the energy needed for hot showers.

The REHPW series comes in 50-, 65-, and 80-gallon sizes. It builds on Rinnai’s existing REHP lineup, with changes designed to make the units easier to install, monitor, and maintain.

In a recent development, heat pump water heaters pull heat from the surrounding air and transfer it into the tank. Moving that heat requires less electricity than producing it with conventional electric resistance elements. There’s no fuel combustion at the appliance, although emissions from its electricity supply depend on the grid.

Rinnai lists a Uniform Energy Factor, or UEF, of 3.75 for the 50-gallon model and 4.0 for the two larger versions. Higher numbers mean greater efficiency under standardized testing; actual bills depend on electricity rates, hot water use, and installation conditions.

The lineup delivers up to 91 gallons of hot water in the first hour, depending on tank size. That rating includes both stored hot water and what the unit can heat during that hour – useful context when several people take consecutive showers.

There are five operating modes, 4.5 kW backup heating elements, and a variable-speed fan designed to keep noise down. The heat pump can operate with ambient air as low as 37°F.

Installation is where some of the more practical upgrades show up.

Sources indicate that the newly introduced Rinnai heat pump water heater units have water connections on both the top and side, giving installers more options for connecting existing plumbing. Both the air intake and exhaust are on top, allowing zero side clearance where Rinnai’s installation requirements permit.

An optional ducting kit adds flexibility for tighter spaces. Carrying handles help with moving the tank into place, and the air filter slides out horizontally from the side for cleaning.

Rinnai has also added a third tank temperature sensor to the 50- and 80-gallon models to help manage hot water delivery.

It has been revealed that wifi adds remote monitoring and control. Rinnai’s updated Central app supports the REHPW series, including scheduling and tools to use time-of-use electricity rates to manage energy use.

In a recent development, the units also carry CTA-2045 AC Level 2 certification for demand response. That gives compatible utility programs a way to communicate with the water heater and adjust its electricity use. Rinnai says the certification can help qualify homeowners for local and state utility demand-response rebates; availability depends on the program.

Sources indicate that the series is Energy Star certified, meets NEEA Tier 4 requirements, and complies with California’s Title 24 requirements, including JA13, according to Rinnai. Warranty coverage includes 10 years for the tank and other parts, plus one year for labor.

Recent findings suggest that I’m very happy with my hybrid heat pump water heater. I run it in heat pump only mode in summer and it helps cool the house for free. For anyone on the fence, especially your utility offers a rebate, it’s definitely worth looking at.

Rinnai directs buyers to an installer for pricing, so the upfront cost – and how much a local rebate might offset it – will require a quote. However, the REHP series price on Amazon hovers around the $2,000 mark.

Industry News: Tesla Cybercab orders open at $29,990 + $299/mo, only in Robotaxi zones

📅 14 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1049 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Electrek

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Tesla is now inviting “select customers” to buy a Cybercab for personal use at $29,990, but the car won’t move unless you also pay $299 a month for an “Autonomy Subscription.”.
  • And it only works inside Tesla’s Robotaxi service areas in Texas and Florida, the same geofences that have turned out to be significantly smaller than what Tesla advertises.
  • Tesla’s official Robotaxi account announced the invites on X on Friday with screenshots of the order page and the invitation email.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Tesla is now inviting “select customers” to buy a Cybercab for personal use at $29,990, but the car won’t move unless you also pay $299 a month for an “Autonomy Subscription.”.

And it only works inside Tesla’s Robotaxi service areas in Texas and Florida, the same geofences that have turned out to be significantly smaller than what Tesla advertises.

Tesla’s official Robotaxi account announced the invites on X on Friday with screenshots of the order page and the invitation email.

The order page lists the Cybercab at $29,990 before taxes, with an estimated delivery of December 2026 in Austin, Texas. You need to put down a $1,000 non-refundable deposit to order.

The subscription isn’t optional. It’s pre-checked on the order page at $299 per month, with one month included, and the fine print notes “Subscription and regular vehicle maintenance required to operate.”.

Sources indicate that the email is even more direct. Its asterisk reads: “Only available in supported service areas. Subscription required for operation.”.

The rest is what we already knew. Two seats, a 21-inch center touchscreen, 20.1 cubic feet of cargo space, and no steering wheel or pedals. Tesla calls it “fully autonomous” and says you’ll “manage your ride in the app.”.

Recent findings suggest that musk had promised a Cybercab “below $30,000” when he unveiled it in 2024. He technically hit it. He just didn’t mention the $3,588 a year it takes to use it. Over five years, that’s about $47,600 for a two-seater, before insurance, maintenance, taxes, and charging.

Recent findings suggest that tesla runs its Robotaxi service in eight cities: Austin, Dallas, Houston, Fort Worth, and San Antonio in Texas, and Miami, Orlando, and Tampa in Florida. That’s where a Cybercab can operate. Everywhere else, it’s a $30,000 sculpture in your driveway.

According to recent reports, and those service areas aren’t what Tesla says they are. Independent tracker Koby Pierce tested thousands of addresses in the Robotaxi app and found that the areas where Tesla actually accepts pickups and drop-offs are only 59% to 78% of the advertised geofences in the six cities he checked. In Austin, the very city where Tesla is delivering these cars, it’s about 59%.

Railroad crossings are a big reason why. In Houston, the creator of Robotaxi Tracker found the app quoting about 40 minutes to go two blocks downtown because the vehicle appeared to route around rail crossings. Tesla also lists San Antonio’s airport inside its polygon but doesn’t serve it.

According to recent reports, then there’s the regulatory cloud. NHTSA has ordered Tesla to prove under oath that a car with no brake pedal meets federal safety standards that require one. Tesla answered on October 30 and asked that the entire response be kept confidential. NHTSA hasn’t ruled. Tesla is now selling the car to consumers anyway.

I think this is going to be a total mess. It looks like Tesla is only doing this by invitation and delivering it in Austin to prove they can deliver an “unsupervised” vehicle in 2026.

Tesla is going to sell these to fans who are excited about owning a self-driving car, and many of them will find out the limitations aren’t worth $299 a month on top of a $30,000 car.

According to recent reports, sure, if your monthly Uber bill is well over $300 and you live and work deep inside the geofence, maybe the math works on paper. Until you realize you have to park it somewhere once you get to your destination. Or that it can’t take you to a friend’s place two neighborhoods over. Or that a 15-minute drive turns into an hour because the car won’t cross a train track. With an Uber or a Waymo, that’s someone else’s problem. With a Cybercab, you’re paying for the privilege.

No point trying to calculate what it will cost over X years. Tesla can change that monthly fee at will anyway (and shall be expected to, considering their overall pricing history).

According to recent reports, and here’s the part that makes no sense to me. The Cybercab runs on the same AI4 computer as the current Model Y. Tesla already runs unsupervised Model Y Robotaxis in these same geofences. So why can’t the Model Y owners who already paid for “Full Self-Driving” get unsupervised operation in those same zones? Wouldn’t be even easier to turn that on these vehicles which have accumulated much more data? Tesla keeps pushing that to “next year,” currently around Q2 2027, while asking people to buy a newly introduced two-seater that can do nothing else.

Recent findings suggest that if the tech works unsupervised in Austin, turn it on for the Model Y owners in Austin. If it doesn’t, why should anyone pay $47,000 over five years for a car that only works where Tesla states it does?

Like with every other Tesla product lately, the delivered version is going to be a lot more disappointing than the one that was sold on stage.

ACOG Strongly Recommends Hormone Therapy for Menopause Symptoms

📅 20 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (908 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Healthline

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (ACOG) published updated recommendations for menopause management in Obstetrics & Gynecology on October 15.
  • Sources indicate that these expanded recommendations are the most comprehensive guidance to date.
  • According to the ACOG guidance, 50%–92% of females experiencing menopause report VMS.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (ACOG) published updated recommendations for menopause management in Obstetrics & Gynecology on October 15.

Sources indicate that these expanded recommendations are the most comprehensive guidance to date. They include fresh clinical guidelines for menopause hormone therapy (MHT), nonhormonal medications, and nonpharmacological treatment of vasomotor symptoms (VMS), which include hot flashes and night sweats, and sleep and mood changes.

According to the ACOG guidance, 50%–92% of females experiencing menopause report VMS.

Around 16%–66% of females in the United States report menopause-related sleep complications, and more than one-third of perimenopausal and postmenopausal females report experiencing depressive symptoms.

“In recent years, misconceptions about the risks of hormone therapy have been widespread, which has made some clinicians reluctant to prescribe it and some patients hesitant to use it,” Bruce Pier, MD, clinical professor and associate fellowship director at the University of North Carolina and collaborator on the ACOG clinical practice guidelines, told Healthline.

“This guidance offers a comprehensive review of the evidence to support individualized counseling and shared decision making. Our hope is that it clears up those misconceptions and expands access to treatment.”.

The ACOG is also developing companion guidance for genitourinary syndrome of menopause, expected in 2027.

The ACOG strongly recommends the use of MHT with estrogen and progestogens (or estrogen alone for people without a uterus) for both VMS and vasomotor-related sleep disturbance, in individuals who can use hormones.

It also conditionally recommends conjugated estrogen plus bazedoxifene (Duavee) as an alternative for these issues.

Sources indicate that according to a meta-analysis from 2021 that was cited by the guidelines, estrogen therapy, with or without progestogens, significantly reduced VMS frequency and severity compared to a placebo or no treatment. A 2017 meta-analysis ranked transdermal estradiol plus a progestogen as the most effective option for reducing VMS frequency.

A 2022 systematic review and meta-analysis, also cited by the guidelines, found that MHT was associated with improved self-reported sleep quality. Once again, transdermal therapies indicated some of the largest effects.

The ACOG recommends initiating MHT before age 60 or within 10 years of the onset of natural menopause..

In a recent development, it also suggests that the decision to start MHT for VMS and vasomotor-related sleep disturbances should be based on a shared decision making discussion about an individual’s symptoms and the benefits and risks of therapy. Consideration should also be taken regarding an individual’s:.

Research demonstrates that factors such as race, culture, socioeconomic status, gender identity, and sexual orientation can influence how individuals experience menopause and the care they receive.

According to the SWAN study, Black women reported more menopause symptoms than white women but were less likely to be treated for them.

“This updated document shines a light on these inequities. Clinicians can proactively help right now by asking every patient in midlife about symptoms, rather than waiting for them to bring it up. Long term, we hope this document drives more research funding to understand these gaps and begin closing them,” noted Pier.

The ACOG stated in the guidelines that, “The available evidence is insufficient to recommend for or against the use of estrogen–progestogen or estrogen-only MHT for the treatment of menopause-related depressive symptoms.”.

It recommends that perimenopausal and postmenopausal individuals who meet the diagnostic criteria for major depressive disorder (MDD) or those whose most noticeable symptom is depression should be treated according to depression management guidelines.

Current treatment guidelines for depression include therapy, medication, or a combination of the two.

Psychological treatments for depression include psychotherapy, such as cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT), while antidepressants are among the most commonly prescribed medications.

The ACOG strongly recommends the use of selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) and serotonin and norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors (SNRIs) for the management of menopausal symptoms like VMS and depression in individuals who don’t want to use MHT or can’t use it.

Right now, paroxetine is the only antidepressant that is approved by the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) for the management of VMS.

The ACOG also strongly recommends the use of neurokinin receptor antagonists to manage VMS and vasomotor-related sleep disturbances in people who don’t desire hormone therapy or can’t use it.

There are currently two neurokinin receptor antagonists approved by the FDA to manage menopause symptoms. Fezolinetant (Veozah) was approved in 2023 to help manage hot flashes. In 2025, the FDA approved elinzanetant (LYNKUET) for the management of moderate to severe VMS due to menopause.

Another nonhormonal treatment for VMS that the ACOG conditionally recommends is gabapentin.

According to recent reports, there are various nonpharmacologic treatments that the ACOG conditionally recommends for the management of VMS, vasomotor-related sleep disturbances, and mood changes. These are treatments that don’t involve the use of medications.

The nonpharmacologic treatments conditionally recommended include:.

It is generally recommended that these interventions are used alongside hormonal or nonhormonal medications.

The ACOG noted that there is not enough evidence to support the efficacy or safety of phytoestrogens, such as soy isoflavones, or herbal supplements, which are not regulated by the FDA in the same way medications are for safety, purity, or efficacy.

Recent findings suggest that “Menopause is finally getting the attention it deserves, and this document shows what evidence-based care should look like in this space. It lays out a range of safe, effective options for managing menopause symptoms. My message to anyone struggling with these symptoms is simple: talk to your clinician. You don’t have to suffer through them,” mentioned Pier.

#75548. Industry News: I finally got a USB-C charging e-bike, and it costs 75% less than Rivian’s bike

📖 Baca
